twi: Asase terew, na Onyàmè ne panyïn.
eng: Of all the wide earth, the Supreme Being is the elder.

twi: Onyàmè
eng: Deriv. given by natives, onyã, to get, and mẽ, to be full, satiated, (by metonymy the sky, which is looked on as his abode).

twi: Onyankõpɔn
eng: The derivation of this word as Onyàmè-nkõ-pɔn (Onyàmè, alone, great one) seems borne out by noting the word in the Akyem dialect, where it is Onyan-koro-pɔn, (Onyàmè, one, great).

twi: Tweaduampɔn
eng: The derivation of this is almost certainly twere-dua-ampɔn (lean on a tree and not fall).

twi: Bore-Bore
eng: Derivation bọ ade, bọ ade (make things, make things), Creator.

twi: Qtumfo
eng: Tumi, power, to be able, and fo the personal suffix.

twi: Onyankõpɔn Kwame
eng: That Onyankõpɔn who was born on Saturday, or came into existence on a Saturday.

twi: Odõmaŋkõmã
eng: Deriv. unknown, but the word is used somewhat as the equivalent of 'inventor'.

twi: Ananse kokõrko
eng: The Great Spider, see note on No. 175 on ananse.

twi: Obi kwan nsi (or ntwa) obi kwan mu
eng: No man's path crosses another man's path

twi: Wope akã asem akyere Onyankõpoŋ a, kã kyere mframa.
eng: If you wish to tell anything to the Supreme Being, tell it to the winds.

twi: Obi nkyere abofra onyàmè.
eng: No one shows a child the sky.

twi: Obi nkyere otomfo ba atono ; onim atono a, Onyàmè na okyeree no.
eng: No one instructs the son of a smith how to forge ; if he knows how to forge, it is the Supreme Being taught him.

twi: Onyankõpoŋ ammã asonomfõa katakyi biribi a, omãã no ahõdannañ.
eng: If the Supreme Being gave the swallow nothing else, He gave it swiftness in turning.

twi: Osansa se, ‘Ade a Onyàmé aye ṅhĩna ye’.
eng: The hawk (poised aloft) says, ‘All things that the Supreme Being made are beautiful (good)’.

twi: Me a meda ayannya miṅhũ Onyankõpoṅ, na wo a wubutuw ho!
eng: I, who lie on my back looking upwards, do not see the Supreme Being, so what do you expect who are sprawling there on your belly!

twi: Onyankõpoṅ mpe aṣemmone, nti na okye diṅ mmiakõ-mmiakõ.
eng: Because the Supreme Being did not wish any bad words, He gave a name to each thing, one by one.

twi: Onyàmé ṅkrabea nni kwatibea.
eng: The destiny the Supreme Being has assigned to you cannot be avoided.

twi: Wokra Onyankɔ̃pɔn a, obi nnyina ho
eng: When you take leave of the Supreme Being, no one stands by

twi: Onyàmé ayi no, asamaŋfo ayi no
eng: The Supreme Being has driven him out, the spirit folk have driven him out

twi: Asem a Onyàmé adi asie no, oteasefo nnaṅ no.
eng: The fate (lit. words) that the Supreme Being has beforehand ordained, a human being does not alter.

twi: Onyankõpoṅ ṅkum wo na odasãni (oteasefo) kum wo, wuṅwu.
eng: If the Supreme Being does not kill you but a human being kills you, you do not die.

twi: Onyankõpoṅ hye wo nsã kora mã na oteasefo kã gu a, ohyia wo so bio.
eng: When the Supreme Being fills your gourd cup full of wine and a human being (comes and) pours it away, He will fill it up again for you.

twi: Onyàmè mã wo yare a, omã wo aduru.
eng: If the Supreme Being gives you sickness, He (also) gives you medicine.

twi: Onyàmè na owo basin fufu mã no.
eng: It is the Supreme Being who pounds the fufu for the one without arms.

twi: Nnipa ũlãnã ye Onyàmé mma, obi nye asase ba.
eng: All men are the children of the Supreme Being, no one is a child of the earth.

twi: Odõmaŋkõmã bo owu mã owu kum no.
eng: The Creator created death (only) for death to kill Him.

twi: Obosom a onnii guan da, ohũ guan aniwam' mpẽ a, ose, 'Eye srade'.
eng: The fetish that has never had a sheep given to it, when it sees even the matter in the corner of a sheep's eye, says 'It is a fat one'.

twi: Onyàmè.
eng: A Supreme Being (see No. 1).

twi: Abosom.
eng: 'Fetishes', i. e. spirit, power, mana from or of the Supreme Being.

twi: Suman.
eng: Minor deities, deriving their power from the abosom.

twi: Suman.
eng: Amulets or charms, a lower grade of the above (3).

twi: Asaman.
eng: A spirit world, inhabited by asamanfo spirits (see note on No. 34, osaman).

twi: Bayifo.
eng: Witches and wizards, human vampires (see No. 56).

twi: Bonsam.
eng: Monsters, half human, half devil (see note on No. 56, sasabonsám).

twi: Obosom a oyẹ nnam na odi aboadé.
eng: The fetish that is sharp (clever at predicting events) is the one that has offerings vowed to it.

twi: Obosom Kyeré nantwi, womfá mfa abonteŋ, womfa mfa afikyiri, nso ewo nea wodé fá.
eng: The fetish Kyere's cow is not taken down the street, and is not led behind the town, nevertheless a way is found to take it.

twi: Obosom anim, woko no mperensã.
eng: One goes before a fetish as often as one likes.

twi: Obosom so, yeŋko no mperensã.
eng: One is not taken before a fetish a great number of times.

twi: Abosom na ɛkyerɛ akomfo ntwahõ.
eng: It is the fetishes who show the fetish priests how to turn when dancing.

twi: Obosomaketere hye ohye a, ohye.
eng: If the fetish lizard (chameleon) is predestined to be burned, it will be burned.

twi: Obosomfó kã ne ṅkõnim, na ʋṅkã ne ṅkőgu.
eng: The fetish priest tells of his victories, but not of his defeats. (That is, boasts of his successful prophecies, but says nothing about the unfulfilled ones.)

twi: Eto sikyi ō, eto mfuaté ō, yenyã okomfo kum no.
eng: Whether the die falls sikyi or whether it falls mfuaté, we are going to kill the fetish priest.

twi: Owu de ne pasũa fa ofi mu a, obosomfo aduru dan nsu.
eng: When death encamps over against a household, the medicine of the fetish priest turns to water.

twi: Okomfo uni ṅkontoro na wontwa obosonsofo ti.
eng: When the fetish priest has given a false prophecy, the fetish carrier's head is not cut off.

twi: Akomfo aduasã fĩre oyarefo a, wodi atoro.
eng: When thirty fetish priests are looking after a sick man, (some of them) are lying.

twi: Sika nti, na okomfo mene agyan.
eng: For the sake of gold dust, the fetish priest swallows an arrow.

twi: Obi ṅkyerẹ ọkọmfo ba akọm.
eng: No one shows the child of a fetish priest how to dance.

twi: Akọkọ wọ ṅkwã adurŭ a, aṅkã yẹde no tẅa abọsọm sọọ?
eng: If a fowl possessed life-giving medicine, would it be taken and sacrificed over fetishes?

twi: Adurŭ a ẹfi kọmfọ nsam' ṅhĩnã yẹ aduru-pa.
eng: All the medicine (charms) that come from the hands of the fetish priest are good (real) charms.

twi: Obi mfa ntẅahõ nsisi kọmfọ.
eng: No one deceives a fetish priest by dancing.

twi: Oteasefo na omã osaman kon do otó.
eng: It is the living man who causes the denizen of the spirit world to long for the mashed yam.

twi: Osamaṅ-twẽn-twẽn.
eng: A spirit or ghost that is seen at intervals by living persons.

twi: Woye ‘me-ńko-medi’ a, wunyã osamaṅ ńhũi.
eng: If you are an ‘eat-by-myself’ person, you will often see a spirit.

twi: Osamaṅ-pa hyira ne ba.
eng: A good spirit (ghost) looks after its child.

twi: Nsamampow mu soduru, wo nĩ wu a, wo abusũa asã.
eng: Bent stick in the spirit grove, when your mother is dead that is the end of your family.

twi: Wo nĩ wu a.
eng: Lit. when your mother dies, in this case when the parent tree, on which the hooked stick grows, is cut or falls down.

twi: Oyere (plu. -nom)
eng: Wife

twi: Agya (lit. father)
eng: Uncle (paternal)

twi: Wofa
eng: Uncle (maternal)

twi: Ena
eng: Aunt (maternal)

twi: Osewa
eng: Aunt (paternal)

twi: Wofasewa
eng: Niece

twi: Wofase
eng: Nephew

twi: Oba (lit. child, son, or daughter)
eng: Child

twi: Oba (lit. child, son, or daughter)
eng: Niece

twi: Oba (lit. child, son, or daughter)
eng: Nephew

twi: Onua
eng: Cousin

twi: Agya ne nua ba
eng: Cousin

twi: Nana (Nana-barima, Nana-ba)
eng: Grandparent

twi: Oba nana
eng: Grandchild

twi: Nanankanso (lit. 'Grandparent not touch (his) ear')
eng: Great-grandparent

twi: Ase
eng: Father-in-law

twi: Osew
eng: Mother-in-law

twi: Akonta
eng: Brother-in-law

twi: Okunu (lit. husband)
eng: Brother-in-law

twi: Oyere (nua) (lit. wife)
eng: Sister-in-law

twi: Akumma
eng: Sister-in-law

twi: Nĩwamma nsae a, wofase uni ade
eng: When (one's) mother's children are not finished, (one's) nephew does not inherit.

twi: Osamane ahõfĩwam ne nunúm.
eng: The smell of a ghost is the smell of the 'nunúm' shrub.

twi: Osamañ tẽe ne nsa kyia wo a, wopono wo de mu.
eng: When a ghost puts forth its hand to greet you, you draw your's back.

twi: Osamañ ṅtẽeñ teasefo ansã-na wadidi.
eng: A ghost does not wait for the living to begin to eat before it begins to partake.

twi: Asamañ nni biribi a, ɛwọ ṅhyehye-wo-ákyi.
eng: If the spirit world possesses nothing else, it has at least the power of its name.

twi: Asamaŋ, woŋko nsaŋ mma.
eng: The spirit world is not a place one can visit and return from again (as a living man).

twi: Asamaŋ, wommănã.
eng: Things cannot be sent to the spirit world (?). (Meaning obscure.)

twi: Asamantawa se enim pae a, ɛte sɛ atawa pa.
eng: When the ‘spirit’ tawa tree declares it knows how to pop, at best it can hope to do so (only) like the real tawa tree (if as well even as that).

twi: Onipa wu (wɔ) samampow mu a, womfá no mma ofie bio.
eng: When a man dies in the spirit grove (cemetery), he is not brought back to the home again.

twi: Wunni samaŋ aduaŋ a, womfa wo nsa nto mu.
eng: If you are not going to partake of the spirits’ food, do not put your hand in it.

twi: Wubu wɔ sumáŋ asumammá a, ekita wo.
eng: If you call your amulet a trifling thing, it will seize hold of you (kill you).

twi: Opanyiṅ ano seṅ sumaṅ.
eng: The advice (lit. mouth) of a man of ripe experience is more potent than (your) little guardian deity.

twi: Sumaṅ kafirmã nye biribi a, na eye amĩade.
eng: If the little kafirma charm is good for nothing else, it is at any rate an adornment.

twi: Enni bãbiara a wotrã ẅe yisa hinam sumaṅ so a, enye nnam.
eng: There is no special place where one should sit and chew guinea pepper and blow it out over one's tutelary deity, to make it a sharp (clever) little amulet.

twi: Obi mfa nea wawu sumaṅ ṅkã se, ‘Mã me ṅkwã nè akwãhõsaṅ’.
eng: No one takes the amulet of one who has died (and whom therefore it has failed) and addresses it, saying, ‘Give me life and health’.

twi: Wo kra nye a, na wunyã asafo nsam' amanne.
eng: If your soul is not a lucky one, you fall into the hands of a ‘company’.

twi: Ṅkrabea nhĩnā usé.
eng: All destinies are not alike.

twi: Wode wo kra kaw, na woantua no a, ofa wo abufuw.
eng: If you are in debt to your soul, and have not paid it, (your soul) gets angry with you.

twi: Obi ṅkwati Tanno nko aka ase.
eng: No one consults the lots without calling on (his) fetish (lit. Tanno).

twi: Sasabonsám kò ayi a, osɔe obayifo fi.
eng: When a sasabonsám (devil) goes to attend a funeral, he lodges at a witch's house.

twi: Asasabonsam
eng: The asasabonsam is a monster of human shape, living far in the depths of the forest, and only occasionally met by hunters. It sits on tree-tops and its legs dangle down to the ground and have hooks for feet which pick up any one who comes within reach. It has iron teeth. There are female, male, and little sasabonsam. A large fungus growth very like a big cabbage in appearance often found growing on trees is called sasabonsam kyew. i. e. devil's hat.

twi: Ayi
eng: Burial, funeral. Deriv. yi, to take away, to remove. (For custom of burying slaves, wives, &c., with a dead master, see note on No. 467.) The grave is a deep trench from 6 to 8 feet deep in one side of which a cavity is again dug, forming as it were a room, with three walls. (Cf. the Chinyanja mudzi, 'village' or last home.) The body is placed in this case, which is then fenced or screened off. Chiefs and men of importance are buried in the house in which they die, which then becomes their tomb.

twi: Obayifo
eng: Deriv. bayi, sorcery (synonymous term ayen), a wizard, or more generally witch. A kind of human vampire whose chief delight is to suck the blood of children whereby the latter pine and die. Men and women possessed of this black magic are credited with volitant powers, being able to quit their bodies and travel great distances in the night. Besides sucking the blood of victims, they are supposed to be able to extract the sap and juices of crops. (Cases of coco blight are ascribed to the work of the obayifo.) These witches are supposed to be very common and a man never knows but that his friend or even his wife may be one. When prowling at night they are supposed to emit a phosphorescent light from the armpits and anus. An obayifo in everyday life is supposed to be known by having sharp shifty eyes, that are never at rest, also by showing an undue interest in food, and always talking about it, especially meat, and hanging about when cooking is going on, all of which habits are therefore purposely avoided. A man will seldom deny another, even a stranger, a morsel of what he may be eating, or a hunter a little bit of raw meat to any one asking it, hoping thereby to avoid the displeasure of one who, for all he can tell, is a witch or wizard. (See No. 76.) The obayifo can also enter into animals, &c., c. g. buffalo, elephant, snakes, and cause them to kill people. The obayifo is discovered by a process analogous to the 'smelling out' of witches among the

twi: Sasabonsám té ase, wose oye obayifo, na menne se osi odum atifĩna odum nso sow mmoatia.
eng: When a sasabonsám devil is down on the ground he is called a wizard, how much more when he is perched on top of an odum tree, and the odum tree is also bearing a crop of tailless monkeys as its fruit.

twi: Sɛ odum osi hɔ a, ose oyɛ Otanno, na obonsam abesi so . . . .!
eng: When an odum tree stands there, it declares it is Tanno, but when a devil comes and perches on it . . . .!

twi: Owu a akum wo nã nè wo agya vọ hɔ a, wunnye diṅ sɛ, ‘Aka me ṅkõ’.
eng: When Death which has killed your mother and your father is there (with you again), you do not say to him, ‘I alone remain’.

twi: Owu bekum wo se nè wo nĩ a, nsũ sɛ, ‘Me se nè me nĩ awu’, na sũ sɛ, ‘Me nè m’agya nè me nã bɛko’.
eng: If Death has come and killed your father and your mother, do not weep, saying, ‘My father and my mother are dead’, but weep and say, ‘I and my father and my mother will go (with you)’.

twi: Owu bekum wo na wofre no agya a, obekum wo, wofre no eṅã a, obekum wo.
eng: If Death comes to kill you and you supplicate it, calling it ‘Father’, it will kill you, and if you supplicate it, calling it ‘Mother’, it will kill you.

twi: Owu adare nnoŋ fãkõ.
eng: Death's sickle does not reap one place alone.

twi: Owu ṅhĩnã ye owu.
eng: All the different forms Death takes are just the one Death.

twi: Owu na wannyã bābi aŋkọ a, na ọkọ asāmaŋ.
eng: When Death has no particular place to go to, then it goes off to the world of spirits.

twi: Owu nè wo ase hyẹ wo adwuma-yẹ a, owu de na wokọ kaŋ.
eng: If both your father-in-law and Death appoint a day for you to do some work, it is Death's you will go about first.

twi: Owu to wo a, wunse se, ‘Fwẹ aberewa!’
eng: When Death overtakes you, you do not say to it, ‘Look, there is an old woman (take her)!’

twi: Owu wo okyẹkyẹfo adaka ano safẹ.
eng: Death has the key to open the miser's chest.

twi: Owu nye pia na woadi mu ahyemfiri.
eng: Death is not a sleeping-room that can be entered and come out of again.

twi: ‘Mirewu kyẹna, mirewu ne’, na yede ye ayie?
eng: ‘I am going to die to-morrow, I am going to die to-day,’ do they begin the funeral custom (because of such words)?

twi: Wurewu a, wunse se, ‘Mirewu ō! mirewu ō!’
eng: When you are (really) dying, you do not say, ‘Oh, I am dying! Oh, I am dying’!

twi: Obi nim nea owu wo a, aŋkã onsi ho ara da.
eng: If one could know where Death resided, one would never stop there.

twi: Nea wahintiw awu no, wontutu ’mirika ṅko n’ayi ase.
eng: When a man has met his death through having stumbled (fallen), one does not run to attend the funeral of such an one.

twi: Qkom nye Krakye Dente nye.
eng: Hunger is not good (good, in sense of, ‘to be lightly thought of’), neither is Krakye Dente.

twi: Obayifo ba wu a, eye no yaw.
eng: When a witch's child dies, it makes her sad.

twi: Obayifo oreko e! obayifo oreko e! na wonye obayifo a, wuntwa wo ani.
eng: A witch is passing! a witch is passing! (some one cries), but if you are not a witch you do not turn your eyes to look.

twi: Obayifo kum wadi-wamma-me, na onkum wama-me-na-esua.
eng: The sorcerer kills (by magic) the one who eats and gives him nothing, but he does not kill him who eats and gives him (even) a little piece.

twi: Efunu a ebesi nnim sudew.
eng: The corpse which is coming to knock against (some one) cares nothing for cries of sorrow.

twi: Kontromfĩ se, ‘Qberan wu né kóko’.
eng: The monkey says, ‘The brave man dies because of his brave heart’.

twi: Kontromfĩ se, ‘Afei ne ampa’.
eng: The monkey says, ‘Well now I shall really speak the truth’.

twi: Kontromfĩ se, ‘Me suman ne m’aniwa’.
eng: The monkey says, ‘My talisman (against surprise and enemies) is my little eyes’.

twi: Kontromfĩ se, ohũa ayi akyẽafo adi.
eng: The monkey says that there is nothing like poverty for taking the conceit out of a man.

twi: Kontromfĩ se, ‘Wohye m’afonom’ a, na meyi asempa makã makyere wo’.
eng: The monkey says, ‘If you fill up my cheeks (with food), then I shall reveal the truth and tell you’.

twi: Yenim se kontromfĩ koŋ wo ho, na yede hãmã to n’aseŋmu.
eng: We know the monkey has a neck, but we nevertheless take a string and attach it to its waist.

twi: Obi ṅhyẹ kontromfĩ mmã onni soṅ.
eng: No one compels a monkey to eat the tamarind (?) fruit. (The oṣoṅ, tamarind (?), is the favourite food of monkeys).

twi: Oduahyeṅ se, ‘Nea ewo m'afonom nye me dea, nea ako me yam' na eye me dea’.
eng: The white-tailed one (the black colobus monkey) says, ‘What is in my cheek is not mine, but what has gone into my belly that is my very own’.

twi: Kontromfĩ akwakorā na oware kontromfĩ aberewa.
eng: It is Mr. Old-man-monkey who marries Mrs. Old-woman-monkey.

twi: Kontromfĩ kyẽa senea akyẽafo kyẽa, nso ne to kō.
eng: The monkey struts about just as a conceited person does, but its bottom is red nevertheless.

twi: Mahũ kontromfĩ a ne yerɛ awu na wasiw atimum, na wo wansaŋ de, efa wo hɔ dɛn?
eng: I have seen a monkey whose wife has died and he has let his hair grow long in consequence, but as far as you are concerned, Bush-buck, how does it concern you?

twi: Esóno akyi nni aboa.
eng: After the elephant there is no other animal (to compare with it in size and strength).

twi: Esóno akyi aboa ne bòmmofó!
eng: After the elephant is a (still greater) animal, the hunter!

twi: Esóno kuntaṅ na adowa di panyiṅ.
eng: The elephant is big and bulky but the (little) duyker has most experience and sense.

twi: Esóno nni wuram' a, ankã ekó ye obopoṅ bi.
eng: If the elephant were not in the jungle ('bush'), then the buffalo would be one of the greatest of the beasts.

twi: Esóno tia afiri so a, eṅhũaṅ.
eng: When the elephant treads on a trap, it does not spring (on it).

twi: Okáka bu sono sê.
eng: Toothache breaks the elephant's tusk.

twi: Nea esóno wui n'afikyiri no, eho ahaban ṅhĩnã sãe.
eng: Where an elephant died, all the leaves in his backyard were spoiled. (Trampled down by people coming to cut up the meat.)

twi: Osekaṅ-tiá biako ṅṅuá ɛsóno, ṅṅua ko, ṅṅua oḍeṅkyem-mirempɔṅ, na wasaṅ agua oṅaṅkã, na wasaṅ atwa wo wura nsa, na woṅhɔṅ wo nto ade mu ana?
eng: One little knife which cannot flay an elephant, which cannot flay a buffalo, which cannot flay a big-throated crocodile, and yet you have gone out of your way (lit. turned back) to flay a python, and gone out of your way to cut your master's hand, will you not be plucked from your handle and cast into some place (out of the way)?

twi: Esóno di asãwa.
eng: An elephant eats the (little) asãwa berries.

twi: Esóno afɔṅ a, woṅné mpakam-mã ọha.
eng: When an elephant is thin, that is not to say its meat will not fill a hundred baskets.

twi: Esóno afɔṅ a, woṅṅua no berew so.
eng: (Even) when an elephant is thin, it is not skinned on a palm leaf.

twi: Esóno hɔ na wọbọ apuruwá.
eng: It is from the elephant that big lumps of meat are cut.

twi: Esóno kàkrã, na adowa na ọde ne ha.
eng: The elephant is a huge beast, but it is the duyker that is the (real) king of 'the bush' (jungle).

twi: Esóno nyã wo a, adowa bọ wo mẽ.
eng: When the elephant has got you in his clutches, the (little) duyker (comes up) and slaps you.

twi: Obi nnyae sóno akyi di ṅkodi aseredoa akyi.
eng: No one gives up following an elephant to go and follow the little aseredoa bird.

twi: Obi nni sóno akyi mmoro hũãsú.
eng: No one (who) is following an elephant has to knock the dew off the grass.

twi: Wudi sóno akyi a, wontõa.
eng: When you follow an elephant you do not get entangled (with creepers).

twi: Obiakõfo na okum sóno, na amansaṅ ṅhĩnã di.
eng: It is one man who kills an elephant, but many people who eat its flesh.

twi: Ebia wobedi sóno na biribi ṅhĩa wo, na wudi apatã a, na dompe ahĩa wo.
eng: Perhaps you will eat a whole elephant and nothing will stick in your throat, and then you eat a (little) fish and lo! a bone has stuck in your throat.

twi: Wode kokŭrokó na edi amim a, ankã esóno beba ofie.
eng: If mere bulk and size could be used to further greed and violence, then the elephant would have come to the haunts of men (to seize what he wanted).

twi: Wode sóno ṅhõma bu kotuku, na wode deṅ ahyem'?
eng: You may make a bag out of an elephant's hide, but what are you going to find to put in it?

twi: Obi nnim nea esóno di yee kese.
eng: No one knows what the elephant ate to make it big.

twi: Obi nsusu sóno yam' mmu ahaban.
eng: No one breaks off a leaf in order to measure the size of an elephant's belly with it.

twi: Enye aduan na esono nya di kyeṅ adowa nti na oye kese seṅ no.
eng: It is not the greater amount of food that the elephant eats than the duyker that makes it greater in size than he.

twi: Womfá akărā ntow sóno.
eng: A wax (bullet) is not used to shoot an elephant.

twi: Gyata dōsō ṽiram' a, aṅkā nnipa nnyā bābi ntrā.
eng: If lions were very numerous in 'the bush', then man would have no place to stay.

twi: Woboro gyata a, wo tiri pā wo.
eng: If you strike a lion, your own head will pain you (you will not do the lion any harm).

twi: Gyahene hō nye deṅ a, onné kaṅkaṅ.
eng: Even when a lion is not a strong lion, it is not called a civet cat.

twi: Ade hĩa osebo a, owe wura.
eng: When a leopard is hard pressed for food, it chews grass.

twi: Obi nkyerɛ osebo ba atow.
eng: No one teaches a leopard's cub how to spring.

twi: Wode sebɔ ǹhõma sũa adw̌inni a, na wode aẅie.
eng: When you use a leopard's skin for practising leather work on, it shows you have mastered your trade.

twi: Osu fĩwe sebɔ a, ne hɔ na eḟow, na ne ṅwǎrǎṅ-ṅwǎrǎṅ de, empopa.
eng: When rain beats on a leopard it wets him, but it does not wash out his spots.

twi: Eko kum Krǎnni a, meṅko no ayi, na Okrǎnni kum 'ko a, minni ne nãm.
eng: When a buffalo kills an Accra man, I do not go to his funeral, and when an Accra man kills a buffalo, I do not eat its flesh.

twi: Otũẽ dua ye tia a, nea ode pra nehõ ara nẽ.
eng: The duyker's tail may be short, but it brushes its body with it notwithstanding.

twi: Otũẽ nhõma suane nea eye hare.
eng: The duyker's skin (hide) splits where it is thinnest.

twi: Otũẽ anko gua, ne nhõma ko.
eng: The duyker does not go to market, but its skin does.

twi: Otũẽ ne otũẽ kõ na wohũ gyahene a, na woko afa na woguan.
eng: When two duykers are quarrelling, and they see a lion (coming), off they run together (forgetting their quarrel).

twi: Otũẽ ani ansen a, na efi bommofo.
eng: When the antelope is unhappy, it is the hunter who is the cause.

twi: Otĭwẽ nyã nantu a, wokyi.
eng: When (you see) a duyker which has a (thick) leg, that is something you avoid (make a taboo).

twi: Otĭwẽ m'pŏrow adu kŭrom!
eng: Let the antelope rot in the hollow of the tree! (A congener of our 'dog in the manger'.)

twi: Odeŋkyem da nsu mu, nso ọnom mframa.
eng: The crocodile lies in the water, but it also drinks (breathes) the air.

twi: Odeŋkyem weree sene were-pá de.
eng: A crocodile's skin is sweeter than any other skin.

twi: Funtumfrafu deŋkyem frafu, wowo yafunu koro nanso wonyã biribi a, wofom, nanso woŋ nhĩnara wo yafunu koro, nanso wodi no amenemutwitwi.
eng: The 'Two-headed crocodiles' have but one belly for both, yet when either of them get anything they fight among themselves for it, for though they both have only one belly for each of their separate heads, each wants the food to pass down its own throat.

twi: Wutwa asu wie a, na wuse odeŋkyem ano pow.
eng: When you have quite crossed the river, you say that the crocodile has a lump on its snout.

twi: Okótó a oda siká hõ po twĕre abé.
eng: Even the crab, that lives where the gold dust is, eats palm nuts.

twi: Okótó ṅwo anõmã.
eng: A crab does not give birth to a bird.

twi: Okótó bene asuo 'ti na onim asuo kasā.
eng: Because the crab lives near the river he knows the language of the river.

twi: Okótó bo pemmo a, osaṅ n'akyi.
eng: When a crab falls down plump on its bottom, it turns back.

twi: Okótó foforó aperew mu nni nãm.
eng: A young crab has no meat in its claws.

twi: Okótó guaṅ a, oguaṅ ko pom'.
eng: When a crab runs away it is towards the sea it flees.

twi: Okɔtɔ́ na onim sika dabere.
eng: It is the crab that knows where the gold dust is to be found.

twi: Okɔtɔ́ annyã adayé nti na oda amɔ̃a mu.
eng: Because the crab has no good place to sleep in, it lives in a hole.

twi: Okɔtɔ́ po di sukɔm, na menne okwaku a oda osoro.
eng: Even the crab gets thirsty, not to speak of the monkey that sleeps up above.

twi: Aboa dompɔ nni asumguarede nti na ɔnam asu hɔ̃ bɔ akɔtɔ́.
eng: Because the otter (?) has made no preparation for the washing of its soul, that is why it walks about digging for crabs (to offer to the soul).

twi: Koṭókó reko koṭókó a, omfa adidide.
eng: When the porcupine is going to visit the porcupine, he does not take any food with him.

twi: Aboa akyekyereɛ nni ntuma, nsoso awow nne no da.
eng: The tortoise has no cloth, hair, or wool, nevertheless it does not ever feel the cold.

twi: Mmoadõmã ńhĩnã foro bo, akyekyere ń'koforo bi, wapoṅ afĩwe.
eng: All animals (can) climb stones, but let the tortoise try to, and he tumbles down. (Said of an unlucky person.)

twi: Akyekyere nni nufu, uso owo a, onim nea oye yeṅ ne ba.
eng: The tortoise has not any milk, but when it gives birth, it knows how to rear its child.

twi: Akyekyere ko serew serew na oguaṅ ara neṅ.
eng: The tortoise goes off in a laughable manner, but he can escape all the same.

twi: Akyekyere na okyere ne bobere na woho no.
eng: It is the tortoise itself that exposes its vulnerable spot (the head) and has it struck.

twi: Akyekyere pe ne yere amanne, ose, ‘Wow m’akyi mmeṣã (wow mmeṣã gu m’atiko), ná meṅkofĩwe agoru’.
Akyɛkyere se, ‘Obarima mfɛre aguan’.
eng: The tortoise says, ‘A man need not be ashamed to run away’.

twi: Akyɛkyere se, ‘Ntɛm ye, na odɔm ye’.
eng: The tortoise says, ‘Haste is a good thing and deliberation is also a good thing’.

twi: Nhwi nye-nã a, ankã akyɛkyere nni bi?
eng: If hair was not difficult to grow, would not the tortoise have some?

twi: Woko awuru kũrom’ na odi dɔte a, wudi bi.
eng: When you go to the village of the tortoise and it eats earth, you eat some oo.

twi: Awuru rewea (na) ne ba rewea, (na) hena na obegye wɔn tãtã?
eng: The tortoise crawls, and his child crawls, and which will take the other and teach him how to walk upright?

twi: Okétɛw a otare pɔdɔ hɔ bo ye tow-nã.
eng: It is difficult to throw a stone at a lizard which is clinging to a pot (without breaking the pot).

twi: Okétέw nὲ ketebɔ sε diŋ na wɔnsέ hɔnam.
eng: The lizard (okétέw) and the antelope (ketebɔ) have names which are similar, but their appearance is not the same.

twi: Okétέw nim sε ayanikaw bεba nti na obutuw siei.
eng: Because the lizard knows its belly will become painful, it lies down on it (before the pain comes).

twi: Okétέw wo yam aduru a, aŋkã yam ansi no adurade.
eng: Had the lizard medicine against eczema, then its body would not be clothed with eczema.

twi: Okétέw ńwε mako na fifiri mfi atǐwεrɔrɔ.
eng: The lizard does not eat pepper and sweat break out on the frog. (A man bears the brunt of his own actions.)

twi: Ńwaw de nehɔ sie a, na wofa no tope.
eng: If the snail takes care of itself, when it is taken, it will be taken as a big snail.

twi: Ṅwaw wu ṅkwaṅ mu a, empŏrow.
eng: When a snail dies in the soup, it does not rot.

twi: Ọwọ de ahõyerew na ọka.
eng: It is owing to being disturbed that a snake bites.

twi: Ọwọ aduru, wọtew no ahõọhare.
eng: The herbs to apply to a snake bite are quickly plucked.

twi: Ọwọ ṅka onipa kwa.
eng: A snake does not bite a man without a cause.

twi: Ọwọ ṅkesua ṅkõ na ebesuw wuram' a, aṅkã biribiara nseee ẹ.
eng: If it were only snakes' eggs that were addled in 'the bush', that would not have mattered at all.

twi: Ọwọ te sẹ hãmã, na wọmfa ṅkyekyere ade.
eng: A snake is like rope, but it is not (for that reason) taken to bind a thing with.

twi: Aboa naṅkã nim adekyẽe a, aṅkã ọda ṅwia-da?
eng: If the python knew when it was dawn, would it sleep in the day-time?

twi: Wọnhũ ọwọ ti a, wọmmọ no abã.
eng: Unless you see a snake's head, you do not strike at it (any other part of the body).

twi: Ọnankanini da ase anyã ọṅwãm.
eng: The python lies on the ground and has got a toucan.

twi: Aboa ananse nam na ọso ne daṅ.
eng: The spider walks and carries his house (web).

twi: Ananse a ọmpe aṅwene bi aṅwene, na ọṅwene tempoṅ mu.
eng: A spider which does not really wish to spin spins its web on a much frequented road (where the people passing soon break it).

twi: Ananse se asantrofi se, ‘Se wobɛfiri aseɛ so a, firi aseɛ so, se wopɛdi ŋkorowa hene a, firi ŋkorowa hene so di’.
eng: The spider says to the night-jar (!) ‘If you are going to look after the beans, look after the beans, but if you are going to be leader in the ŋkorowa dance, then confine your energies to that’ (lit. be leader in the ŋkorowa dance).

twi: Ananse antoŋ kasa.
eng: The spider has not sold words.

twi: Agya Ananse adi asɛmmɔne na yepam no, na wannya babi ankoro na ɔseɛ padeɛ ani.
eng: Father Spider did wrong and we drove him away, and as he had no place to go he hangs from the crossbeams of the roof.

twi: Agya Ananse ṅwoo ne ba Ntikũmã na owo nea oso ne boto.
eng: Before Father Spider begot his son Ntikũmã he had some one to carry his bag.

twi: Efere nti na agya Ananse de otwẽ kyew hye adow.
eng: Because of shame Father Spider takes an antelope skin hat when he goes to ask people to come and assist him at his hoeing.

twi: Mireguare suohyew na ananse reguare ne mma, na meguare suonwini e?
eng: I bathe in hot water, and the spider keeps washing his children in it, so I shall wash in cold water and what can he do then?

twi: Obi ntó anansesem ṅkyere Ntikũmã.
eng: No one tells stories to Ntikũmã.

twi: Ńwansana de ne nsa gu n'akyi a, ose, ‘Nea aka akyiri na ɛdɔsõ’.
eng: When the fly stretches his legs (lit. hands) behind him, he says, ‘There still remains a lot to come’ (lit. what is behind is much). If one watches a fly closely it will sometimes be seen to stretch its feet backward over its body. This proverb is used in the sense of ‘I have done a great deal for you, but you can still hope for future signs of favour.’

twi: Ńwansana ampa funu hɔ a, wode no sie.
eng: When a fly does not get up off a dead body, he is buried with it.

twi: Ńwansana pobi, onni ano, na ótǐwère bebuŋ.
eng: The bluebottle fly (?) has no mouth, but it can strip the green palm nuts.

twi: Ńwansana pobi si abeyā mu a, wotaforo mu.
eng: Though the bluebottle fly sits on the dish, you lick inside it.

twi: Ńwansana ye sisi a, onsi gya mu.
eng: Wherever else a fly is going to alight, it does not alight on fire.

twi: Ohurii di bem, ńwansana na oyę me sē.
eng: Now surely the tsetse had good reason to bite me (as every one knows it is a biting fly), for here is the common house fly doing the same (and it is not supposed to bite at all).

twi: Ohurii nni gyamfo.
eng: The biting fly has no one to come to his aid in trouble.

twi: Ohurii si akyekyere akyi kwa.
eng: The biting fly gets nothing by alighting on the back of the tortoise.

twi: ‘Meka nnipa ṅhĩnā,’ nti na ohurii annyã ogyamfo.
eng: ‘I shall bite all men,’ because of that the tsetse has no one to come to his aid in trouble.

twi: Mfóté pấm ansã-na woaye yā.
eng: Ants have to unite (in great numbers) before they (can) make a noise.

twi: Mfotee te se dǐwie, nanso o nè no nse.
eng: A white ant is like a louse, and yet they are not really the same.

twi: Mfote a wuwu a wobedi wo nãm no, na wote ho a, wowe wo tam.
eng: The white ants that will, when you die, devour your flesh, when you are alive eat your clothes.

twi: Obi ṅkotoa ohãhíni wo né bón anò ná onse se, ‘Wo ho bọ̀n’.
eng: No one tracks a black ant to the mouth of its hole and then says, ‘You stink’.

twi: Obi nnyina ṅkráṅ mù ntutú ṅkráṅ
eng: No one stands among black ants and picks off black ants.

twi: Ṅkesua to ṅkráṅ mu a, mã eṅna mu, na woṅam hõ kwa.
eng: When an egg falls among black ants, let it lie there, for they will walk over it without being able to do it any harm.

twi: Obi nton ne kokobere kwà.
eng: No one sells his (laying) hen without a good reason.

twi: Akoko nom nsu a, ode kyere Onyankõpoŋ.
eng: When a fowl drinks water, it (first) takes it and shows it to the Supreme Being.

twi: Akoko di wo yoŋkõ aŵi a, pam no, na dabi obedi wo de.
eng: When a fowl is eating your friend's grain, drive it away, for some day it will eat yours.

twi: Akoko ani sã bŭrofua.
eng: The fowl's eye is keen to see the single grain of corn.

twi: Akoko se, ‘Ade ansã a, aṅkã memẽe?’
eng: The fowl says, ‘If it had not got dark, should I have had my fill?’

twi: Akoko naṅ ṅkum ba.
eng: The hen's foot does not kill (her) chicken.

twi: Akoko hyeṅ kye ofie a, obere.
eng: When a white fowl remains a long time in a house, it gets red (with earth and dust).

twi: Akoko ntakāra na ɛmã akoko yɛ kese.
eng: It is the feathers on a fowl that make it big.

twi: Akoko ntakāra nyin a, etuatua ne hōnam mu.
eng: When the feathers of a fowl grow, they still remain attached to its body.

twi: Wo kyere akokotaṅ a, wo tase ne mma kwa.
eng: When you have caught the mother hen, you pick up the chickens without difficulty.

twi: Obi ntwa akoko ano mmã akyɛ.
eng: No one says ‘Good morning’ before the cock has done so.

twi: Akokobere nim adekyɛe, na ofiɛ onini ano.
eng: The hen knows when the dawn comes, but she nevertheless looks to the cock (to make it known).

twi: Akokonini bow nsã na ne wɛre afi akōrōmã.
eng: When the cock is drunk he forgets about the hawk.

twi: Akokonini se, ‘To tamfo ṅkō a, aṅkã maboṅ anadwo na woakum me’.
eng: The cock says, ‘Had I nothing but enemies left, then when I have crowed in the night I should have been killed’.

twi: Okokonini, gyae wohõ kyerɛ, na wo nã ne kesua hóno.
eng: O cock, leave off being puffed up with pride; after all, your mother was only an egg-shell.

twi: Obi mfa akokɔ nañase ade, mfa ṅkɔto akokofĩwerew nañase.
eng: No one takes the string of beads off a fowl's leg and goes and puts it on the leg of a partridge.

twi: Akokɔ nni asõ nanso ónnyã ne sõtore a, wode bɔ no ara.
eng: A fowl has no ears, so does not get them boxed, but it gets its beating all the same.

twi: Akokɔ-pa na ɔwo asense, asense (se), ‘Me ṅkɔ mifi hẽ?’
eng: An ordinary fowl hatches out an asense chicken, and the asense one (asks in wonder) saying, ‘I alone, where did I come from?’

twi: Akokɔ se, ‘Kyerɛ akyekyere tutu no’, na ono akyekyere se, ‘Na wo de, woabĕre’.
eng: The fowl says, ‘Catch the tortoise and pluck it,’ but he (the tortoise) replies, ‘As for you, you will (lit. have tired) tire of trying that’.

twi: Akokɔ ti si ahẽ na wɔrebɔ mu fe?
eng: How big is a fowl's head that they should be striking at it?

twi: Okokonini, gyae akuntuṅ-akuntuṅ, na yeṅ ṅhĩnã ye kesua mma.
eng: Cock, desist from self-glorification, for we are all the children of eggs.

twi: Aboa kòkosakyi nni tuo, na oṭoṅ asommeṅ.
eng: The vulture has not a gun, but he sells elephants' tusks.

twi: Aboa kòkosakyi se akasadi nti na oka sumăna so.
eng: The vulture says it is in order to avoid payment (for what he eats) that he remains on the dung-hill.

twi: Aboa akrampã, wudi bi biṅ na obi nni wo de.
eng: Vulture, you eat the excrement of every one, but no one eats yours.

twi: Kòkosakyi akrampã, ne diṅ anye de, na ne hõ anye hũãm.
eng: The vulture has not a good name and its body has not a good smell.

twi: Kòkosakyi mpe ofie aba a, aṅkã onsisi sumăñã so.
eng: If the vulture did not wish to come into the house, it would not stand about on the dung-hill.

twi: Kòkosakyi se, odompo hõ boṅ.
eng: The vulture says that the civet cat stinks.

twi: Opete takŭra tŭa oŭira ṅkontompo a, otu tŭene.
eng: When a vulture's feather tells its master a lie, he (the vulture) plucks it out and casts it away.

twi: Opete hō na eye ṅkwasea, nanso okyi aguare-anni.
eng: A vulture's body is a foolish looking thing, yet even he does not eat without first having had his bath.

twi: Osansa firi ahunum' reba se, ‘Mekokyere nipa madi’, na afei akoŭia akoko.
eng: The hawk comes swooping down from the sky saying, ‘I am going to catch a man and eat him’, and behold! he makes off with a fowl.

twi: Osansa ko abuw a, ode n'akyi gyaw akrōmā.
eng: When the hawk goes to sit on her eggs, she leaves the akrōmā (another kind of hawk) to keep her watch (in the sky).

twi: Akō ntakŭra, se wuhū ne ṅko a, ntow no bo, na ofi dodow mu.
eng: A parrot's feather, if you see but a single one, do not throw a stone at it, for it comes from where there are a great many more.

twi: Akō ano ye deṅ a, obi ṅkyere no nni.
eng: Because the parrot has a loud voice, no one catches hold of it to eat it.

twi: Akō mpe se obi hū ne ṅkesua nti na otow gu duam'.
eng: A parrot lays its eggs in the hollow of a tree because it does not wish any one to see them.

twi: Anõma biakõ wọ wo nsam' a, eye seṅ nnõmã du a ewọ ahunum'.
eng: One bird in your hand is better than ten birds in the sky.

twi: Anõma biara wu wọ soro a, eye deṅ ara a, ne ntakara ba gu fam'.
eng: When any bird dies in the sky, whatever happens (lit. whatever it does), its feathers come falling to the earth.

twi: Anõma bone na osee ne berebuw.
eng: The bad bird fouls its own nest.

twi: Anõma de ako-nè-aba na eṅwene berebuw.
eng: The bird makes (lit. weaves) its nest by going and coming.

twi: Anõma kese antu a, obua da.
eng: When a big (full-grown) bird does not trouble to fly (in search of food), it goes to sleep hungry.

twi: Anõma koro di awi a, otiatia so.
eng: When one bird alone eats the grain, it treads it under foot (there being more than it can eat).

twi: Anõma kye dua so a, ogye bo.
eng: When a bird remains too long on a tree, it has a stone thrown at it.

twi: Anõma nãm ṅkosõ kye.
eng: There is not enough meat in a bird to divide up (among a number of persons).

twi: Anõma ne nua ne nea ọ nè no da.
eng: It is one of its own family that a bird roosts with.

twi: Anõma ano ware a, ode didi asuogya na omfú ntwa asu.
eng: When a bird has a long bill, it uses it for eating on its own side of the river and not for stretching across the water (to eat on the opposite bank).

twi: Okrãmãñ a ọkọ ahayọ wañhũ, na agyinamoa na obẹyẹ dẹñ?
eng: The dog which has gone a hunting has not had any luck, so what can the cat (hope to) do?

twi: Wo krãmãñ se obẹkyere sóno amã wo a, ọdãdã wo.
eng: When your dog says he will catch an elephant for you, he is deceiving you.

twi: Okrãmãñ se oremfa oyere da, na ofa oyere no, ofa n' agya yere.
eng: The dog says he will never commit adultery, but when he does so, he commits it with his own father's wife.

twi: Okrãmãñ ne atiremsẹm da ne bo, na ẹna ne tirim.
eng: A dog's thoughts lie in his chest, but not in his head. (That is, he is always barking (talking) and never keeps anything to himself.)

twi: Obi se wo se, ‘Okrãmãñ ani yẹ anañ’ a, oboa, abieñ yẹ ṅhwĩ.
eng: If any one says, ‘A dog has four eyes’, he is lying, two are (tufts of) hair.

twi: Wo nè krāmãñ bo abusũa a, nisu mpa wo ani ase da.
eng: If you take a dog (i.e. a quarrelsome, noisy person) as a relation, tears will never dry in your eyes.

twi: Okrāmãñ anom ye no de a, oñwe ne koñmu nnawa.
eng: Even when a dog's mouth is watering, he does not gnaw at the bells round his neck.

twi: Okrāmãñ fa kesua a, ebebo wo n' anom.
eng: When a dog picks up an egg, it will break in his mouth.

twi: Okrāmãñ na obu be se, ‘Ade kese nyera’.
eng: The dog has a proverb which runs, ‘A big thing does not get lost’.

twi: Okrāmãñ si pata so na enyé ono na oforee a, na obi na omãã no so sii ho.
eng: When a dog is (found) up on top of the store rack, and could not have climbed up himself, then some one must have lifted and put him there.

twi: Okrāmãñ se, ope 'mirika-húnu atú, na menne se n'ase guan atew ayera.
eng: The dog says he likes to run about without any particular reason; how much faster will he run when he hears his mother-in-law's sheep has broken loose and is lost.

twi: Agyinamoa wo p̃afo a, aṅkã oye nnam kyeṅ krãmãṅ.
eng: Had the cat only some one to help it, it would be sharper even than the dog.

twi: Agyinamoa nam fie s̃e ne kotoku a, anad̃oboa mfa ne nsa ntom'.
eng: When the cat walks about the house carrying his bag, the night animal (the mouse) does not put his hand inside.

twi: Agyinamoa wu a, ṅkura yam'.
eng: When the cat dies, the mice rejoice.

twi: Agyinamoa akoa ne botokura.
eng: The cat's slave is the mouse.

twi: Obi ṅkyere agyinamoa akrommo.
eng: No one teaches a cat how to steal.

twi: Obi ṅkyere agyinamoa apákyi mù fǐé.
eng: No one teaches a cat how to look into a calabash.

twi: Aboa agyinamoa nni biribi, nanso owo ahõohare.
eng: If the cat has nothing else, it has agility.

twi: Aboa agyinamoa nim se ntṷẽmu ye de a, ankã ọtṷẽ ne mu du Abṷrokyiri.
eng: If the cat really thought stretching itself (after a sleep) was a delightful sensation, it would go on stretching and stretching till it reached to Europe.

twi: Oguanteṅ ṅwo aberekyi.
eng: A sheep does not give birth to a goat.

twi: Nea oguaṅ gyinae na ne ba gyinae.
eng: Where the sheep stands its kid stands.

twi: Obi mfa aberekyi nto guanteṅ hṍ.
eng: No one compares a goat with a sheep.

twi: Oguaṅ bewu, na onnyã ṅwui a, wọmfre no guaṅfunu.
eng: When a sheep is going to die, but is not yet dead, it is not called a dead sheep.

twi: Oguaṅ ano kã ṅkyene a, onnyae ẅe.
eng: When a sheep's mouth touches salt, it does not stop eating it.

twi: Oguaṅ funu mpaw ọsekaṅ.
eng: A dead sheep does not choose the knife (it is to be cut up with).

twi: Oguaṅ wuda ye ọdesãni wuda.
eng: The day on which a sheep dies is also the day on which a man dies.

twi: Oguanteṅ se, ‘Mefḭwe ọsebo na mawo no so’.
eng: The sheep says, ‘I shall look on a leopard that I may give birth to one like it’.

twi: Odwɛnnini yɛ asisi a, efiri ne kɔma emfiri ne mmɛn.
eng: When a ram is brave, (its courage) comes from its heart and not from its horns.

twi: Aberekyi se obɛdan guantɛn a, tuntum mpa mu da.
eng: Though the goat determines to turn into a sheep, there will always be a patch of black somewhere.

twi: Aberekyi se, obi nnamtew ṅkowu.
eng: The goat says no one will (willingly) walk to his death.

twi: Aberekyi se, nea abogyabum wɔ no, ɛho na adidi wɔ.
eng: The goat says that where there is much blood, there is food.

twi: Aberekyi se, ‘Woato me nã, na woanto me’.
eng: The goat says, ‘They have bought my mother, but they have not bought me’.

twi: Aboa aberekyi na obu ne bɛ se, ‘Ade pa na wokata so’.
eng: The goat has a saying which goes, ‘A good thing is (sure to be) covered over’.

twi: Nantwi mmɛn ani awo, nso ase yɛ mono.
eng: The outer surface of a cow's horns is hard, but underneath is soft.

twi: Obi ntɔ nantwi nammɔn.
eng: No one buys a cow's footprint.

twi: Ɛnyɛ nantwi ṅkɔ na ofiri Sàruha baa Kumase.
eng: It is not only cattle that come from Salaga to Coomassie.

twi: Opoŋko mmaŋ kwa.
eng: A horse does not turn to the side without a cause. (That is, it is answering to the rein.)

twi: Opoŋko agyimi a, nea ote no so nnyimii e.
eng: Though the horse is a fool, it does not follow at all that the rider is a fool.

twi: Opoŋko aŋko osa a, ne dua ko.
eng: If the horse does not go to war, its tail does.

twi: Opoŋko wo dua, esóno wo dua, na opoŋko de kyeŋ sóno de kākrā.
eng: A horse has a tail and an elephant has a tail, but that of the horse is a little larger than that of the elephant.

twi: Akura te sɛ nantwi a, na agyinamoa akoa ara neŋ.
eng: Even if the mouse were the size of a cow, he would be the cat's slave nevertheless.

twi: Akura se, ‘Nea okum me nye me yaw sɛ nea ode me fiwe fam’.
eng: The mouse says, ‘He who kills me does not hurt me as much as the one who throws me on the ground’ (after I am dead).

twi: Ŋkura dɔdow bɔre tũ a, eŋŋo.
eng: When a great number of mice dig a hole, it does not become deep.

twi: Aboa kisi nyã fufũ a, obedi, na owoma na eŋko ne boŋ mu.
eng: When the rat gets fufu (pounded yam, cassava, &c.), he will eat it, but the pestle (used for pounding it) does not go into his hole.

twi: Okisi kofa adwe na Oŋyàmέ bɔ-ayeremu a, odaŋ atwene.
eng: When the rat goes to eat palm nuts and the Supreme Being flashes the lightning, he throws them away.

twi: Okisi apo adwe.
eng: The rat is tired of palm nuts.

twi: Okisinini aŋhũ adwe-bɔ, na obére bɔ a, owe bi.
eng: When Mr. Rat does not know how to crack a palm-nut kernel, but Mrs. Rat does, he eats some (of her's).

twi: Woko okisi kŭrom' na ọwẹ ṅṅwẹa a, woowe bi.
eng: When you go to the rat's town and he eats palm-nut kernels, you eat some too.

twi: Obi mfi aboa no anim mmọ hama.
eng: No one begins to twist creepers into a rope in front of an animal (he hopes to catch).

twi: Aboa a obẹba nnim waw.
eng: The animal that is coming (towards the hunter) knows nothing about the man lying in wait for it.

twi: Aboa a ne họ wọ nhwi fi fifiri a, wonhũ.
eng: When an animal with a hairy skin sweats, it is not (so easily) noticed.

twi: Aboa bi rẹnka wo a, ọnnwẹn ne sẹ nkyerẹ wo.
eng: When an animal is not going to bite you, it does not show its teeth at you.

twi: Aboa ne nea ọwẹ wura wọ wuram'.
eng: It is the animal that eats grass that lives (is to be found) in the grass.

twi: Aboa no nhintaw nnyaw ne dua.
eng: That animal does not hide and leave its tail sticking out.

twi: Aboa no kaw nea n'ano sõ.
eng: That animal bites wherever its mouth reaches to.

twi: Mmoadõmã ṅhĩnã fi fifiri, na nhwĩ na emmã yẹnhũ.
eng: All animals sweat, but the hair on them causes us not to notice it. The saying is used in the sense that a rich or powerful man can bear losses or troubles better than a poor one, though both may equally have their worries.

twi: Dom gu a, woŋhyeŋ no abeŋ.
eng: When an army suffers defeat a horn is not blown in its honour.

twi: Dom ṅnui a, woṅkaṅ atofo.
eng: The slain are not counted before the (hostile) army has been routed.

twi: Dom, wokõ no abooduru, na woṅkõ no ahĩ-dodow.
eng: An army is driven back by courage and not by insults, however many.

twi: Dom kum ano-sese-ade, na dom ṅkum dommarima.
eng: The (victorious) army slays him who shouts out challenges and insults, but it spares the brave man.

twi: Dom nnim dom akyi.
eng: An army does not know what is at the rear of an army.

twi: Obarima, voye no dom āno, na woṅyé no fie.
eng: A man is made in the forefront of battle and not (by remaining) at home.

twi: Okõ aba a, na nsise aba.
eng: When war has come, rumours have come.

twi: Okõ ba a, na nsise bo kŭrow.
eng: When war comes, it is rumours that cause the fall of the town.

twi: Wokõ, ko wo anim a, na wuyi dom.
eng: When you fight and press on to your front, then you will conquer.

twi: Wokõ ṅkrãṅ na eṅko a, wontwene abe ṅṅu mu.
eng: When you are fighting black ants and they will not go away, you do not peel palm nuts and put amongst them.

twi: Wokõ na wunyi dom a, womfá nnommúm.
eng: When you fight and do not win, you do not lead away captives.

twi: Osa, woko no ṅkatae dodo.
eng: Many gun-lock covers go to war.

twi: Osa, woko no woŋ agya mma.
eng: When one goes to war, it is against one's father's children (i.e. brothers by one father but by different mothers).

twi: Obi nturu yarefo ṅkó 'sá.
eng: No one carries a sick man on his back when going to war.

twi: Obòfó à wókodi nò yaw na otuo apae akã ne nsa yi, na wo de, woso brode bedew reko hẽ?
eng: The hunter to whom you serve as attendant has been wounded in the hand by the bursting of his gun, so, as for you, where are you setting off to with the bundle of plantains?

twi: Obòfó aboa a wafõm no bíara nye ketewa da.
eng: No animal that a hunter has ever missed is small.

twi: Obomofo, a woakum pete (a wonn ine nãm), woasee wo atuduru.
eng: Hunter, who have killed a vulture (the flesh of which cannot be eaten), you have wasted your powder.

twi: Obomofo aboa a oko na osõ.
eng: To the hunter the animal that gets off is (always) the big one.

twi: Obomofo din bata sõnnam hõ.
eng: The hunter's name clings to the elephant's meat.

twi: Obomofo fi wuram ba na okura mmere a, wommisa ahayo mu asem.
eng: When the hunter comes from the bush carrying mushrooms, he is not asked for news of his hunting.

twi: Obomofo ko wuram' mã osu to afiwe no, mã ntummoa keka ne hõ, mã awow ade no, mã ofiwerem' awo no, ne nhinana ye due na mede memãe.
eng: When a hunter goes to the bush and is beaten by the rain, and bitten by flies, and suffers from the cold, and is pricked by thorns, all these hardships are included, when I tell him I am sorry for him.

twi: Obomofo kotew dua na aboa amma a, osan ba ofie.
eng: When the hunter crouches behind a tree, but the game for which he is lying in wait does not come, he returns home.

twi: Obomofo nnim aboa yarefo.
eng: The hunter does not spare (lit. know) the sick animal.

twi: Osu to na obomofo bekum aboa a, efi ne katae.
eng: If the rain falls and the hunter kills an animal, that is thanks to the skin cover of his gun lock.

twi: ‘Gye akyekyere komã agya,’ nso ye ahayo ?
eng: ‘Here take the tortoise and go and give it to father,’ would you also call that hunting?

twi: Enyɛ obi nè bomofo na ekɔɔ wuram'.
eng: No one went with the hunter to the bush (i.e. there is no one to contradict you, for you were alone when it happened).

twi: Otuo nyã otiafo a, na odi abaninsem.
eng: It is (only) when a gun has a man to cock it, that it performs war-like deeds.

twi: Otuo paé kã obomofo a, wommisa nea odi obofo nam.
eng: When the gun bursts and wounds the hunter, the man who happens to eat venison is not blamed for the accident. (Lit. is not asked about it.)

twi: Otuo mpae Abŭrokyiri mmɛkã onipa wo Abibirim'.
eng: A gun does not burst in Europe and wound a man in Africa.

twi: Wo atuo sŭa a, na wo asɛm sŭa.
eng: When your guns are few, your words are few.

twi: Otuo tã hŭaṅ a, na ɛ ne poma sɛ pɛ.
eng: When the lock of a gun is out of order, it (the gun) and a stick are just alike.

twi: Otuo ntow aboa bi nnyae ṅkohyehye aboa bi ĭwere mu.
eng: A gun-(shot) does not wound one animal and cause pain to another animal. (Lit. the skin of another.)

twi: Otuo yera nĭfã mu nà èkofi adoṅteṅ mu a, na eṅkɔɔ bãbi ɛ.
eng: When a gun (a soldier) is missing from the right flank of the battle and appears in the forefront of the fight, it did not go amiss.

twi: Tw̌erebo nti na otuo di abaninsem.
eng: Thanks to the flint-stone the gun performs warlike deeds.

twi: Oba a obeye yiye, wonyen no kete-pa so nko.
eng: The child which is to turn out any good is not reared entirely on (even) a beautiful mat.

twi: Oba se ose, nanso owo abusua.
eng: A child (may be) like his father, but he belongs to the mother's side from which he takes his name.

twi: Oba nsu a, womma no nufu?
eng: Is it only when a child cries that he is given the breast?

twi: Wo ba ne to gu wo sere so a, wode baha na eyi, na womfa osekan ntwa.
eng: When your child's excrement falls on your lap, you wipe it off with dry plantain fibres, but you do not take a knife and cut (the place) off.

twi: Wo ba saw asa-bone a, se no se, ‘Wo asaw nye fe’, na nse no se, ‘Okra, tete gu mu’.
eng: When your child dances badly, tell him, saying, ‘Your dancing is not good’, and do not say to him, ‘(Little) soul, just dance as you want to’.

twi: Wo ba sisi wo kora ba a, enyé, nanso wo kora ba sisi wo ba a, enye.
eng: When your own child cheats your fellow wife's child, that is not right, and when your fellow wife's child cheats your own child, that is not right either.

twi: Oba-bone nnim kasakyere.
eng: A bad child does not take advice.

twi: Nea abofra pe ototo.
eng: What a child wants he buys. (Said of a foolish person who must have everything he sees and fancies.)

twi: Abofra bo ṅwaw na ommo akyere yere.
eng: A child breaks a snail, but he does not break a tortoise.

twi: Osekaṅ-fua na egye nehõ abofra nsam'.
eng: It is the knife-blade without the handle that frees itself from the hands of a child (by cutting him).

twi: Abofra nsam' ade nye hye-nã.
eng: It is not difficult to fill a child's hand.

twi: Woye abofra a, nserew akwatia.
eng: When you are a child, do not laugh at a short man.

twi: Abofra nte ne nã nè n' agya asem a, eye mmusu (... odi aduaṅ a ṅkyene nnim').
eng: When a child does not hear the words of its father and mother, there is misfortune in that (... he partakes of food in which is no salt).

twi: Abofra hũ ne nsa hohoro a, na ọ ne mpanyiŋfo didi.
eng: When a child knows how to wash his hands thoroughly, he and (his) elders (can) partake of food together.

twi: Abofra tŭa fufū a, otŭa nea ẹbẹko n'anom'.
eng: When a child cuts off a piece (of boiled) yam, he cuts off what will go into his mouth.

twi: Abofra kā na ẹŋkọ opanyiŋ nsa, na n'aduaŋ de ẹko panyiŋ anom.
eng: A child's ring does not go on an elder's finger, but as for his (the child's) food it goes into the elder's mouth.

twi: Obi nsoma abofra ńfwẹ n'ani akyi.
eng: No one sends a child on an errand and looks to see if he is pleased or not.

twi: Wọkọ kŭrow bi mu, na d̆wom a mmofra to no na mpanyimfo na ẹto gyaw wọŋ.
eng: When you go into some village, the songs which the children sing, the old folk once sang and left behind to them (that is, tradition is handed down).

twi: Abofra sũ a, wommo no duam'.
eng: When a child cries, he is not bound to a log.

twi: Abofra ye nea wonye a, ohũ nea wonhũ.
eng: When a child does what is not (usually) done, he perceives what is not (usually) perceived.

twi: Abofra ye nea opanyin ye a, ohũ nea opanyin hũ.
eng: When a child does what a grown up person does, he sees what a grown up person sees. (Meaning, he is punished as a grown person is punished.)

twi: Abofra boápa wù a, woboápa sié nò.
eng: When a child pretends to be dying, (the best thing to do) is to pretend to bury him.

twi: Abofra a okọ asu na obọ ahina.
eng: The child who goes for water is the one who breaks the pot.

twi: Abofra bọ mmusu akroṅ a, ofa mu anum.
eng: Out of nine mischievous tricks a child thinks to play on others, he suffers for five of them himself.

twi: Abofra kọda gya na opere hṍ a, ne ntama hyew.
eng: When a child goes to lie by the fire and is fidgety, his cloth catches fire.

twi: Abofra ṅfĩwe ọkwanseṅ ase kwa.
eng: A child does not look into the soup pot for nothing (he expects to be given some).

twi: Abofra ketewa bi te fi kẹse bim' a, mã nò due, na wahũ amanne
eng: When a small child lives (alone) in a great big house, pity him, for he has seen misfortune (that is, he has responsibility beyond his years).

twi: Abofra kotow panyiṅ ṅkyeṅ.
eng: The child squats beside the elder.

twi: Abofra ano ye deṅ a, ode hyeṅ abeṅ, na omfa ṅhyeṅ woadúru.
eng: Even when a child has a strong mouth, he blows a horn with it and not a mortar.

twi: Abofra se okoforo dunsiṅ a mã omforo, na okosõ anim asaṅ aba.
eng: When a child says he is going to climb the stump of a tree, let

twi: Abofra se obeso gya mu, mã onso mu, na ɛhye no a obedaŋ akyene.
eng: When a child says he will catch hold of fire, let him catch hold of it, for when it burns him he will (soon) throw it away.

twi: Abofra se obeye mpanyinne a, mã onye, na ebia obenyã opanyin a, obi nnim.
eng: When a child says he wants to act as if he were already a chief, let him do so; as to whether he will ever become one, that no one knows.

twi: Abofra sika te se anyaŋkôma gya, wotwa so a, na adum.
eng: A child's gold dust is like a firebrand of the anyankoma tree; when it is broken up it soon burns out.

twi: Abofra sũa adwini-di a, enye osebo ŋhôma na ode sũa.
eng: When a child is learning his trade as a leather worker, he does not practise on a leopard's skin.

twi: Mmofra hũ kore a osu ato aboro no a, wose oye opete.
eng: When children see an eagle draggled by the rain, they say it is a vulture.

twi: Mmofra ŋ'kotu a, woaŋhũ tu; mpanyin ŋ'kotu a, wotiatia so.
eng: When children go to pluck them (the mpempema mushroom), they do not do so skilfully; when grown-ups go to do so, they trample on them.

twi: Obi nsoma abofra osoro na oṅhũaṅ' ase antwĕri.
eng: No one sends a child up aloft and then knocks away the ladder from beneath him.

twi: Obi nsoma abofra na ommefa no so abufuw.
eng: No one sends a child on (a difficult) errand and gets angry (if he does not perform it well).

twi: Opanyiṅ fere ne mma a, na ne mma suro no.
eng: When an elder (a parent) is strict with his children, then his children fear him.

twi: Opanyiṅ se ná wanyé à, mmɔfra nsuro no.
eng: When the grown-up threatens to punish, (lit. says) but does not carry out his threat (lit. but does not act), the children do not fear him.

twi: Opanyiṅ kyɛ a, edw̃o.
eng: When an elder portions out the dish, it becomes cool. (A wise (old) man knows how to settle disputes).

twi: Opanyiṅ nyiṅ wo ne batw̃ew.
eng: An elder grows at the elbow (i. e. becomes rich).

twi: Obi ututu anomã ṅkokyerɛ opanyiṅ.
eng: No one plucks a bird and goes and shows it to an elder (to inquire its name).

twi: Opanyiṅ di nsem ṅhĩnã akyi a, oman bo.
eng: If an elder were to follow up every (little) offence (in order to inflict punishment), a people (nation) would (soon) go to ruin.

twi: Opanyiṅ nni abansosem akyi.
eng: An elder gives no heed to idle rumours.

twi: Opanyiŋ a wanyiŋ né nea wako Asante aba, ne nea wako Abŭrokyiri aba, atorofo a ewo omaŋ mu neŋ.
eng: The elder who has grown very old is the one (who says) he has gone to Ashanti and returned; (who declares) he has been to Europe and back, a liar among the people is he.

twi: Opanyiŋ didi adibone a, oyi n'asaŋka.
eng: If an elder eats greedily, (he finds) he has to remove his own dish.

twi: Opanyiŋ due, ‘Mante, mante’.
eng: An elder evades responsibility by saying, ‘I have not heard, I have not heard’.

twi: Opanyiŋ begye me nsam' akoŋŋua a, onnyé asase a mete so.
eng: Though an elder may take from my hand the stool I sit on, he cannot take from me the ground I sit on.

twi: Opanyin mɛ̃ nsòno.
eng: An elder can satisfy his hunger with his intestines. (That is, he has other resources to fall back on when needs be, when hunger (used metaphorically for trouble) overtakes him.)

twi: Opanyiŋ nè mmofra hũ nantew a, wosoa ne boṭo.
eng: When the elder and the children know how to adapt their steps to one another's, they (the children) carry his bag.

twi: Opanyiŋ anim asɛm ye ọkã-nã.
eng: It is not an easy matter to speak face to face with an elder.

twi: Opanyiŋ ano seŋ sumaŋ.
eng: (The words from) the mouth of an old man are better than any amulet.

twi: Opanyiŋ tirim na wóhọ̀n akũmã.
eng: It is on the elder's head that the axe-head is knocked off (the shaft).

twi: Opanyiṅ to asã a, na ewo mmofra de mu.
eng: When the old man's bottom is flat, its fatness has gone to the children.

twi: Opanyiṅ ntõ bo-hyew nto abofra nsam'.
eng: An elder does not roast a hot stone and place it in the hand of a child.

twi: Opanyiṅ ntrã ofie na asadua mfow.
eng: The elder does not sit in the house and (allow) the loom to get wet.

twi: Opanyiṅ wo ṅkwã a, onni mfensã.
eng: Even when an old man is strong and hearty, he will not live for ever.

twi: Mpanyimfo na ebu be se, 'Gya me naṅ', na wonse se, 'Gya me ti'.
eng: Experienced men have a saying, 'Leave my legs alone', but you will not hear them saying, 'Leave my head alone'.

twi: Mpanyimfo se, ‘Maye se wo pei’.
eng: The elder (lit. elders) says, ‘I have done as you (are doing now) once upon a time (or, I was as you are)’.

twi: Se mpanyimfo pe wo atɔtɔ awe a, wunhuruw ntra ogya.
eng: If the old people want to roast and eat you, you do not jump over a fire.

twi: Mpanyimfo ye wo guanŋuan, na se wuguan a, akyin no woserew wo.
eng: When the grown-ups (frighten you to) make you run off, and you do so, afterwards they laugh at you.

twi: Akwakora te ho ansana wowoo panyin.
eng: An old man was in the world before a chief was born.

twi: Aberewa a onni se no n'atadwe gu ne kotokum'.
eng: The old woman with no teeth has ‘tiger’ nuts in her bag. (She may have some reason unknown to you for keeping them.)

twi: Aberewa fwe akoko, na akoko fwe aberewa.
eng: The old woman looks after (her) hens and the hens look after the old woman (by laying eggs and hatching out chickens for her).

twi: Aberewa ko asu a, obeba, na ne ntem na yerepe.
eng: When an old woman goes to fetch water (we know) she will come

twi: Aberewa nim ade a, ónnye ne baṅ.
eng: If an old woman (says) she knows (every)thing, let her put up her own fence.

twi: ‘Makyẽ, makyẽ,’ kum aberewa.
eng: ‘Good morning, good morning,’ (eventually) kills an old woman.

twi: Ohem-mone nni bābi, na osafohene-bone na owo bābi.
eng: There is no such thing anywhere as ‘a bad king’, though ‘a bad vassal chief’ may be found.

twi: Ohene a obekum wo mmae a, na wokaṅ ahene dodow a woasōm?
eng: When the chief who will kill you has not yet come (on the stool), can you count how many chiefs you have served under?

twi: Ohene bi bere so wohu, na obi bere so woáyére.
eng: In one chief's reign skins are treated by having the hairs singed off, in that of another the skins are spread in the sun. (Times and manners change.)

twi: Ohene bedi wo kasa a, efi mamfo.
eng: When a chief is going to compel you to do something, he does so by the authority of the people.

twi: Ohene bekum wo a, ennim ahamatŭẽ.
eng: When a chief is going to kill you, it is useless consulting the lots.

twi: Ohene nè wo kã a, na okum wo.
eng: When a chief and you are on (too) intimate terms, (some day) he will kill you.

twi: Ohene anim na woŋkã, na n'akyi de, wose.
eng: One does not speak out one's mind in the presence of a chief, but behind his back one does.

twi: Ohene nufu dẽsõ a, amansãñ na enũm.
eng: When a chief has plenty of milk, then all people drink of him.

twi: Ohene nyã ahõtrãfo pa a, na ne bere so dwo.
eng: When a king has good councillors, then his reign is peaceful.

twi: Ohene nnyã wo a, na wuse, ‘O nè me kã’.
eng: As long as a chief leaves you alone, you say, ‘He and I are good friends’.

twi: Ohene asõ te se 'sono asõ.
eng: The ears of a chief are as the ears of the elephant (i.e. he hears all that is going on).

twi: Ohene asõ te se soñẽ; emu akwan boro apem.
eng: The ears of a chief are like a strainer; there are more than a thousand ways to them.

twi: Ohene ntam te sɛ bayɛrɛ amɔa, obi ntɔ mu mfa nehɔ tɔtrɔtɔ mfi adi da.
eng: A chief's oath is like the hole a yam is planted in, no one falls into it and gets out again unhurt.

twi: Ohene tamfo ne nea ɔ nɛ no fi mmofraase.
eng: The enemy of a chief is he who has grown up with him from childhood.

twi: Ohene te sɛ odum, onni anim nni akyiri.
eng: A chief is like an odum tree, he has no front and no back.

twi: Ohene ba ntutu 'mirika ṅkofwɛ tiri.
eng: A chief's child does not run to look at a head (that has been cut off).

twi: Ahenkwā di adwene na wadwɛn asɛm.
eng: A chief's servant eats fish and gets ideas.

twi: Ahenkwā na ɔmā ohene hɔ yɛ hū.
eng: It is the chief's servant that causes the person of the chief to excite fear.

twi: Osafohene nsua na wakɔ.
eng: A war captain does not take the oath before going to fight.

twi: Ade a ohene pe na woye ma no.
eng: Whatever a chief wishes is done for him.

twi: Nnipa nhina pe ohene aye, na (woanya?) woannya na wose, mpo ahenni ye yaw.
eng: All men would like to be chief(s), but when they cannot get what they want they declare that even to rule as a chief has its worries.

twi: Ade hia ohene nana a, okita tuo, na onsoa akete.
eng: When a chief's grandson is poor, he holds a gun but he does not carry a mat.

twi: Ade hia odehye a, ehia no kakra.
eng: When a free man lacks something, it is something very big he lacks.

twi: Odehye bo dam a, wofre no asabow.
eng: When a man of noble family is mad, people say he is only the worse for wine.

twi: Odehye din nyera da.
eng: A free man's name is never lost.

twi: Odehye, wodi no apatā, na wonni no sono.
eng: Nobility should be borne as one eats fish (humbly) and not as one partakes of elephant flesh (proudly, and boasting about it).

twi: Odehye ṅyehye, na sika na ehyehye.
eng: Fame of being noble born does not spread abroad, it is the fame of riches that spreads.

twi: Odehye ankõ a, akoa guaṅ.
eng: When the free man does not fight, the slave runs away.

twi: Odehye mu nni abofra.
eng: Among royalty no one is a child.

twi: Odehye, woṅnõa wonni, na sika ne asem.
eng: An ancient name cannot be cooked and eaten ; after all, money is the thing.

twi: Odehye, wompae.
eng: A man of royal blood does not need to have his name proclaimed.

twi: Odehye nsore, wosi no mfensã.
eng: The offering on the grave of one of the royal house is placed there for many years.

twi: Odehye te ho a, akoa nni ade.
eng: When the free man is there, the slave does not take command.

twi: Odehye wu a, akoa di ade.
eng: When a free man dies, a slave succeeds.

twi: Odehye nye abofra na woabo ne din abo owu din.
eng: One of royal rank is not a common fellow that he should have his name coupled with the name of Death.

twi: Akoa mpaw wura.
eng: A slave does not choose (his) master.

twi: Akoa ṅhyẹ nehõ ntu sa.
eng: A slave does not make up his own mind about going to war.

twi: Akoa nim wura.
eng: A slave knows (his) master.

twi: Akoa di guaṅ a, ne hõ guaṅ no.
eng: When a slave eats a sheep, he is in trouble.

twi: Akoa ampow a, na efiri ẅira.
eng: When a slave is not well behaved, the cause can be traced to (his) master.

twi: Akoa nni awu na wonkum owura.
eng: When a slave does not commit murder, his master is not killed.

twi: Akoa nim sɔ̃m a, ofa ne ti ade di.
eng: When a slave knows how to serve (his master well), he is permitted to take his own earnings.

twi: Akoa a onim sɔ̃m di ne wura ade.
eng: A slave who knows how to serve succeeds to his master's property.

twi: Akoa nyã nehõ a, ofre nehõ Sonani.
eng: When a slave becomes a rich (and free) man, he calls himself one of the Asona family (a noble family).

twi: Akoa di fo.
eng: A slave is (as a matter of course) guilty.

twi: Akoa ṅkyere nnannua.
eng: A slave does not point out where good sticks for building are to be found.

twi: Akoa nni mpow kwa.
eng: A slave does not eat the second yam crop without good reason.

twi: Akoa nyansa wo ne wura tirim.
eng: A slave's wisdom is in his master's head.

twi: Akoa sure asuko na womã oko a, oguan.
eng: When a slave has ceased to go for water and is (again) made to go, he runs away.

twi: Akoa te se kyekyire, wode nsu kakra gu no so a, na ahono.
eng: A slave is like unto corn ground into flour; when a little water is sprinkled on it, it becomes soft. (A slave is easily influenced by kind treatment.)

twi: Akoa te se twerebo; enni otuo ano a, enye 'ye.
eng: A slave is like the flint on the striker of the gun which, if it were wanting, would make the gun useless. (He is a necessary member of the community.)

twi: Wo nkoa suro wo anim asem a, wonni nim mma wo.
eng: If your slaves fear (to speak) before your face, they will not gain victories for you.

twi: Nnonkofo banu fure nantwi a, okom kum no.
eng: When two slaves look after (your) cow, hunger kills it.

twi: Ahĩa me na fwe mã me, nti na obi yee akoa.
eng: I am in want, so look after me, that is why some men became slaves (lit. one became a slave).

twi: Owura nè akoa ntam' nni, twẽ mã mentwẽ.
eng: Between master and slave there is no 'pull and let me pull' (no striving for the mastery).

twi: Wo wura tan wo a, na ofre wo akoa dehye.
eng: When your master hates you, then he calls you a free-born slave.

twi: Obi nto akoa na ommehye no so.
eng: No one buys a slave to act as a restraint on himself.

twi: Wunni wura a, obi kyere wo, ton, di.
eng: When you have no master, some one catches you and sells you for what you will fetch.

twi: Wofere wo afana a, wudi nnuanfin.
eng: When you fear to reprimand your slave girl, you eat stale food.

twi: Akoa ohantanni, wode no sie funu.
eng: A proud slave is taken and buried with the corpse (of his master).

twi: Obi nhũ bi kwaberaŋ ṅhuruw nsi.
eng: No one sees a strong slave belonging to another man and jumps for joy about it.

twi: Obi akoa di péreguaŋ na womã asũãsã to no a, oyi kaw sũã mã wutua.
eng: When some one's slave who is worth a péreguaŋ of gold dust (£8) is sold to you for an asũãsã's worth (about £6), he is pretty sure to go and incur some debt for a sũã's worth (about £2) that you will have to pay.

twi: Abusũa ṅhĩnã ye abusũa, na yefwefwe mmetẽmã so de.
eng: All family names are family names (and good enough at that), but we search well between the thorns of the oil palm for the good nuts nevertheless.

twi: Abusũa te sɛ ńfwiren, egugu akuw-akuw.
eng: Family names are like flowers, they blossom in clusters.

twi: Abusũa ye dom, na wo nã oba ne wo nua.
eng: The family is an army, and your own mother's child is your real kinsman (brother or sister).

twi: Abusũa dua, wontwá.
eng: The family tree is not cut.

twi: Nea oman bi kã serew na oman bi kã sũ.
eng: What one people talk and laugh about, another people talk and cry about.

twi: Oman rebebo a, efi afi mu.
eng: When a nation is about to come to ruin, the cause begins in the homes (of its people).

twi: Oman bo, na menné abobow.
eng: A nation is (can be) destroyed, how much more one home (lit. a gate).

twi: Oman Akuapem, wokonyã ade a, wose, ‘Obusufo!’, nso woannyã a, wose ‘Okărabiri!’
eng: The Akuapem people say, when you get wealthy, ‘Mischievous fellow!’, and when you have nothing, they say ‘Unlucky one!’.

twi: Oman kum wo a, na ohene kum wo.
eng: When (the united) people (want to) kill you, then the chief kills you.

twi: Omaṅ te se adesoa, woṅhũ mu ade dakoro.
eng: A people are like unto a load (containing many things), you cannot perceive all the contents in a single day.

twi: Omaṅ tẅa wo sãmã a, wompopa.
eng: When it is the unanimous wish of a people that you dress your hair in a certain way, you are compelled to do so (lit. you do not rub it out).

twi: Omaṅ rebebo a, oṃáṃpám na ókùra pōma.
eng: When a nation is about to come to ruin, then the salamander holds the staff.

twi: Agya, gyae na meŋkã, wokyi.
eng: Father, stop, and let me tell (you what you ought to do), it is not permitted to speak so.

twi: Agya mma nyã a, mepe; eŋã mma nyã a, mepe papāpa.
eng: When (my) father's children get (anything), I like that; when (my) mother's children get (anything), I like that even better.

twi: M'agya dea, mémfa, me nã dea mémfa, na ebere awi.
eng: It is my father's, so let me take it; it is my mother's, so let me take it, that brings (a child) to stealing.

twi: Wo agya akoa twa dua a, wuse, ‘Eye merew’.
eng: When your father's slave cuts down a tree, you say, ‘It is soft wood (easy to cut)’.

twi: Wo nã ba ne Kobuobi a, ankã wobese sɛ kyene kɛse fata no ana?
eng: Even if your mother's son is 'Kobuobi', would you tell him that the big drum was a fit thing for him to carry?

twi: Wo nã oba ne wo nua.
eng: Your mother's child is your kinsman (brother or sister).

twi: Wo nã di hĩa a, wunnyae no ṅkofa obi nye nã.
eng: When your mother is poor, you do not leave her and go and make some one else your mother.

twi: Wo nã aṅkõ gua a, na womãnã wo nã né kòra.
eng: When your own mother does not go to market, then your step-mother is sent.

twi: Wo nã wu na wobeye ayi a, didi wie ansã, na ṅkoto piti na wo ani ṅkowu mpanyimfo anim.
eng: When your mother has died and you are about to celebrate the funeral custom, finish eating first, lest you go and faint and shame yourself before the elders.

twi: Wo nã awu a, wo abusũa asã.
eng: When your mother dies, you have no kindred left.

twi: Wo nã nye a, na wo nã ara neñ.
eng: Even if your mother is not a good woman, she is your mother nevertheless.

twi: Wudi wo agya akyi a, wusũa ne nantew.
eng: When you follow behind your father, you learn to walk like him.

twi: Wunni nã na woko obi fi agoro a, na otu ne mma fo a, wode tu wohõ bi.
eng: When you have no mother and you go to some one's house to play, and she (the mother) admonishes her children, you profit by some of that advice yourself.

twi: Agorũ a ɛreba wo nã nè wo agya abóbów ano nó, wompe ntem ṅkofwe.
eng: The dance which is coming to your mother's and your father's door, you do not go off in haste to look at elsewhere.

twi: Wokã wo agya a, wokã wo nã bi.
eng: When you swear the oath of your father, you should also swear that of your mother.

twi: Memeneda Koromante
eng: Koromante Saturday

twi: ntam kese
eng: the great oath

twi: Akantamansu
eng: oath from the name of a battle near Dodowa

twi: Wukuda
eng: Wednesday's oath

twi: Abañakyi
eng: lit. after or behind the castle, castle being used as the personification of the English Government; this oath referring to the last rising in 1900 in Ashanti

twi: sepow
eng: a skewer-like knife used to pierce through both cheeks of a man about to be executed to prevent him from 'swearing the king's oath'

twi: Obosom nkum ohene
eng: May a fetish kill the king

twi: edwira
eng: the sacred (blessing or sprinkling) on the king

twi: Obi mfi bea akyi ntu ne tam.
eng: No one can pull the loin-cloth off a woman without her knowledge.

twi: Obea ko aguare na wamma ntem a, na osiesie nehõ.
eng: When a woman goes to bathe and is a long time in returning, then (you can be sure) she is decking herself out.

twi: Obea tenten so abɛ a, oŋwam di.
eng: When a tall girl carries palm nuts, the toucan eats (them).

twi: Mmea ǹhĩnã ye bākõ.
eng: All women are alike.

twi: Mmea n'nyae ankā aguare, na ahohow hõ bọ̀n.
eng: Let women cease to bathe with limes, for even the (ahohow) red ant has an offensive smell.

twi: Mmea pẹ nea sika wo.
eng: Where the gold dust is, that is where the women like to be.

twi: Mmea se, ‘Wo hō ye fe’ a, ene ka.
eng: When the women say (to you) ‘You are a handsome fellow’, that means you are going to run into debt.

twi: Obā hō ye fe a, efi ne kunu.
eng: When a woman is beautiful, it is from her husband she gets her beauty.

twi: Obā na onim kunu.
eng: It is the woman who knows her husband.

twi: Obā nyinsen na waṅwo bā a, owo baniṅ.
eng: When a woman conceives and does not give birth to a girl, she gives birth to a boy.

twi: Obā tĭwa bommā a, etv̆eri barima daṅ mu.
eng: Even when a woman makes (lit. cuts) a drum, it leans against the man's house.

twi: O-ba-yi-fo, o-do-man-ko-ma, kye-re-ma se, o-re-se-re, wo, ba-bi, a-gyi-na.
eng: O wizard, the sacred drummer says he craves of you a place to stand.

twi: Twe-re-bo-a, Ko-di-a, Bi-rim-pon, o-do-man-ko-ma, kye-re-ma, se, o-ko-o, ba-bi, a, wa-ma ne ho m-me-re-so, fir-im-pon, da-mir-i-fa, da-mir-i-fa, da-mir-i-fa!
eng: O cedar tree (from which the drum is made), the mighty one, the divine drummer says he had gone elsewhere for a while, but that now he has returned, pity, pity, pity.

twi: O-bu-a, yen-kye-re-du, o-do-man-ko-ma, kye-re-ma, se, o-ko-o, ba-bi, a, wa-ma ne ho m-me-re-so fi-rim-pon, da-mir-i-fa, da-mir-i-fa, da-mir-i-fa!
eng: O obua tree (from which the pegs are cut that hold down the skin), the divine drummer says he had gone elsewhere for a while, but now he has returned, pity, pity, pity.

twi: Bo-fu-mu, am-pa-se-kyi, o-do-man-ko-ma, kye-re-ma se, . . . (as before).
eng: O bofumu apasekyi (the tree from which the bark is stripped to make the string with which the skin is fastened down to the pegs), the divine drummer says . . . (as before).

twi: A-fe-ma, dun-si-ni, ne, a-sa-re n-kon-ta, o-do-man-ko-ma kye-re-ma, se . . . (as before).
eng: O afuna tree (from which the drumsticks are cut), the divine drummer says . . . (as before).

twi: E-so-no, o-bu, a-ku-ma, o-do-man-ko-ma, kye-re-ma, se, . . .
eng: O elephant (lit. the great one), breaker of the axe, the divine drummer says . . .

twi: A-si-a-ma-To-ku-A-sa-re, o-twe-a-du-am-poŋ, o-nyà-mé, o-do-man-ko-ma, kye-re-ma, se, o-ko-o, ba-li, a, wa-ma, ne-ho, m-me-re, so, o-bo-o, de-en, o-bo-o o-seŋ, na, o-bo-o, o-kye-re-ma, na o-bo-o, o-bra-fo ti-ti-ri.
eng: Asiama-Toku-Asare (the first king who sat on the stool of Mampoŋ), Supreme Being, God, the divine drummer says he had gone elsewhere, but has now returned. What did He create; He created the herald, He created the drummer, but above all He created the executioner.

twi: O-do-man-ko-ma, bo-o, a-de, Bo-re Bo-re bo, a-de, o-bo de, e-beŋ, o-bo-o o-seŋ, o-bo-o, kye-re-ma, o-bo-o, Ku-a-ku, Ak-wa, bo-a-fo ti-ti-ri Ko-nin-sa-mo-agya, Gya-me, A-mo-a-gya e-seŋ, be-gye, wo, fo-kye, o-gya, wo de e-beŋ o-gya, wo, a-ka-bu, o-gya, wo a-to-per-e o-gya, wo, Gya-me, A-m-poŋ-sa-kyi, A-m-pon-sa, Mam-poŋ, A-som Gyi-ma, bi-rem-poŋ fi-rim-poŋ, da-mir-i-fa, da-mir-i-fa, da-mir-i-fa !
eng: The Supreme Being created things, the Creator created things, what things did He create? He created the herald, He created the drummer, He created Kwaku Akua (meaning unknown), but chiefly He created the executioner, Koninsamoagya, Gyame, Amoagya

twi: Wo yere a onye no, na ete se obi aguaman.
eng: When your wife is a woman of no morals, then she might as well be some one else's harlot.

twi: Wo yere anyin a, wuntutu 'mirika na ɛkohyia no.
eng: Before your wife has reached puberty you do not run to meet her.

twi: Wo yere nom anum a, wo tɛkrɛma anum.
eng: When you have five wives, you have five tongues.

twi: Wo yere apem a, wo asɛm apem.
eng: When you have a thousand wives, you have a thousand 'palavers'.

twi: Obea nɛ ne kunu asɛm, obi nnim mu.
eng: The conversation between husband and wife no one knows about.

twi: Oyere te sɛ kũntũ; wòdè katá wo sò a, wo hɔ̃ keka wo, wuyi gu hɔ nso a, awɔw de wo.
eng: A wife is like a blanket; when you cover yourself with it, it irritates you, and yet if you cast it aside you feel cold.

twi: Oyere nye nãm na woakyekye amãnã.
eng: A wife is not meat that she should be parcelled up and sent out to others.

twi: Wo yere nye a, ɛnte sɛ wo ǹkõ wo da.
eng: Even if your wife be a bad lot, that is not to say you are going to sleep alone.

twi: Asɛm a wontumi ǹkã no abɔntɛn so no, wo nè wo yere te fie a, ǹkã ǹkyerɛ no.
eng: When you have anything to say which could not be spoken on the street, do not tell it to your wife when you and she are together at home.

twi: Woko na obi nè ne yere rekõ a, mpɛ ntɛm mmua, na ɛwo nea wayɛ no.
eng: When you go (to a man's house) and find him fighting with his

twi: Nea orefwɛfwɛ yere nto mmea hɔ mpɛ.
eng: One who is looking out for a wife does not speak contemptuously of women.

twi: Aware foforo sa ode.
eng: On the honeymoon the yams always taste sweet. (Lit. (in) a new marriage, the yams mix well.)

twi: Wowo ba bone a, wofa okasabɛre.
eng: When you give birth to a bad child, you (will) grow weary of speaking.

twi: Wowo nipa, na woawo ne tamfo.
eng: A man is brought forth; his enemy has (already) been born.

twi: Wowoo tafoni ba no, na onkura ta.
eng: When the archer was born, he did not hold a bow.

twi: Mawo wo mabɛre, wokyi.
eng: 'I am weary of having born you' is something no one ever wants to say.

twi: Obi nhyee da nwoo panyin peŋ.
eng: No one ever yet fixed on a particular day to give birth to an elder (i. e. a man who was to be of importance some day).

twi: Wowoo ‘ Wo di amim’ Kwasida, na wowoo ‘ Wo yi adwɔw’ Dwɔda.
