eng: The greedy person was born on Sunday and the extortioner on Monday.

twi: Ohoho akyi mpa asem.
eng: After a stranger has gone there is always something to be said about him (good or bad).

twi: Ohoho ama woanya sika ama woanya kaw.
eng: A stranger causes one to get money (but) he also is the cause of one getting (bad) debts.

twi: Ohoho ani akese-akese, nanso enhu man mu asem, na nea ode kurow aniwa nkete-nkete na ohu mu asem.
eng: A stranger may have big big eyes, but he does not see into what is going on among the people he is among, whereas the town's man, with little little eyes, he knows all the town's affairs.

twi: Ohoho nsoa funu ti.
eng: A stranger does not carry the head of the corpse.

twi: Ohoho soe wo fi na wannyaw wo biribi a, ogyaw wo kaw.
eng: When a stranger stops at your house and does not leave you anything else, he leaves you debts.

twi: Ohoho te se abofra.
eng: A stranger is like a child.

twi: Ohoho te se sunsuansu.
eng: A stranger is like unto the water running over the ground after a rain storm (which soon dries up and leaves little trace behind.)

twi: Ohoho nto mmara.
eng: A stranger does not break laws.

twi: Ahohoduan ye wo de a, wo anuonyam ye ketewa.
eng: When you accept the hospitality of a stranger, your dignity is small.

twi: Aburokyiri nye ko-na, na po na ehua.
eng: It would not be difficult to go to Europe, if it were not for the sea.

twi: Aburokyiri a mereko ehua me, mpoano na ehua me.
eng: (The thought of) Europe, where I am going, does not distress me, it is (surf on) the beach that is the difficulty.

twi: Nnipa nhina pe Aburokyiri ako, na onya na wonnya.
eng: All men would like to go to Europe, it is the opportunity they lack.

twi: Oburoni a ote abantenten mu, se owu a, na oda fam'.
eng: The white man who lives in the castle, when he dies he lies in the ground.

twi: Obŭroni toŋ asekaŋ na ne ti afuw.
eng: It is the white man who sells knives, yet his head is overgrown with hairs.

twi: Brofo adaworoma na yeṅ ṅhĩnā furafura ntãmã.
eng: It is thanks to the white man that we all wear cloths.

twi: Brofo de nyansa na eforo po.
eng: By virtue of wisdom the white men mount the sea.

twi: Obrọfotefo na ọmā obŭroni ye aye.
eng: It is the native who knows English who directs the white man whom to praise (and whom to blame).

twi: Obi nim se ohĩa behĩa no a, aṅkã oko Brofo mã 'yewo no.
eng: If any one had knowledge previous to his birth that he was going to have to suffer from poverty, then he would have gone to the white men that he might have been born of them. In the native mind all Europeans must be prosperous and rich.

twi: Wudi Bŭroni ade a, woko aprem ano.
eng: When you eat the white man's pay, you fight at the cannon's mouth.

twi: Wo nã te Abibirim' na wo agya te Abŭrokyiri, na wope ade a, woṅkye nyã.
eng: When your mother lives in Africa and your father in Europe, and when there is a thing you want, you do not have to wait for it.

twi: Ọkọm de aberewa a, na ose, ‘Tọt õ biribi mã mmofra na wonni’.
eng: When an old woman is hungry, then she says, ‘Roast something for the children that they may eat’.

twi: Ọkọm de họho a, oda, na odidi mẽ a, obisabisa nkũrofo yerenom.
eng: When a stranger is hungry he sleeps, but when he has eaten his fill he goes about accosting the town's folks' wives.

twi: Ọkọm de họho a, ode fi ne kũrom.
eng: When a stranger is hungry, he brought it (hunger) with him from his own village.

twi: Ọkọm de akoa, na okọm de hene.
eng: Hunger is felt by a slave and hunger is felt by a king.

twi: Ọkọm de wo a, ede wo nkõ.
eng: When you feel hungry, it is only you who feel hungry (one does not feel hungry for another).

twi: Ọkọm de wo a, womfá wo nsa abién nnidi.
eng: When you are hungry, you do not use both your hands for eating with.

twi: Ọkọm nè ka, na efanim ka.
eng: Of (the two) hunger and debt, debt is preferable.

twi: Oyare a ebekum wo bo wo a, wonkae duruyofo.
eng: When the illness that is going to kill you comes upon you, you forget the doctor who could have cured you.

twi: Qyare, wokõ no ahohora.
eng: Illness is driven off by insults (fear of insults)?

twi: Qyare nsãe a, wonnye ayaresade.
eng: The physician's fee is not paid till the sickness is over.

twi: Qyare see akyẽafo.
eng: Sickness destroys even he who is most worthy.

twi: Woyare anomdew a, na woyare ntoto.
eng: If you suffer from a complaint that is always crying out for delicacies, then you (also) have a complaint that is always calling for buying.

twi: Oduruyefo nnõm aduru mmã oyarefo.
eng: The physician does not drink the medicine for the patient.

twi: Wopa opayare a, oyare pa gye wo mu.
eng: When you make pretence of being ill, a real illness lays hold on you.

twi: Obi nyaré ayamka ṅkye akyebŭro mfa nsa nehõ yare.
eng: No one who has belly-ache tries to cure himself with parched corn.

twi: Nnua ṅhĩnã ye aduru, na wunnim a, na wuse, eye bone.
eng: All plants are medicinal, but you do not know and say this one is (useless) bad.

twi: Mâ me aduru mprempreŋ, nye aduru.
eng: Give me medicine at once, you cannot expect that to be good medicine.

twi: Suro nea obeŋ wo.
eng: Fear him who is near you.

twi: Suro nea ose, obegye, na nsuro nea ose, ‘Meremã wo’.
eng: Fear him who says he will take from you, but do not fear him who says, ‘I am going to give you’.

twi: Misuro kum nti na maye me koŋ tiã.
eng: Because I fear to be killed I have made my neck short.

twi: Yensuru dom anim, na menne asem anim.
eng: We do not fear the front of battle, much less the front where words are weapons.

twi: Wusuro nnimmo a, wode wo sekaŋ gua oŋaŋkã.
eng: If you are afraid to incur unpopularity, you have your knife taken (borrowed) to flay a python.

twi: Wusuro odoŋko bi a, wofwɛ no mpreŋsã.
eng: When you fear (to remove) a slave's excrement, you look on it many times.

twi: Wusuro guamsem a, wo abaguade ye ketewa.
eng: When you fear to take part in public disputes, your share of fees (for attending such 'palavers') is small.

twi: Wusuro ahenware a, wowo nnofowa ba.
eng: If you fear to marry a chief, you will give birth to a nameless child.

twi: Wotaṅ wo yoŋkõ ba a, wo ba wu awusiṅ.
eng: When you hate your friend's child, your own child dies a sudden death.

twi: Wotaṅ nipa a, womã oye nneema ṅhiṅã.
eng: When a man is disliked he is blamed for all kinds of things.

twi: Obi taṅ wo a, na oparuw wo mparuṅwoma.
eng: When some one hates you, he makes malignant remarks about you.

twi: Obi taṅ wo a, eṅworaṅwora wo.
eng: When some one hates you, he scratches you.

twi: Obi taṅ wo a, na obọ wo aboa ade.
eng: When some one hates you, he reminds you of the promises you made (and have not fulfilled).

twi: Wo atamfo abieṣã ko agyina, na hena na abebu wo bem ?
eng: When three people who hate you go aside to deliberate on the verdict to be given on you, who is going to find you innocent ?

twi: Wo tamfo di wo aṣem ase kaṅ a, wokã ṅkyene a, edaṅ mako.
eng: When one who hates you gets the first chance to state a case he has with you (before the elders), when you talk salt it turns to pepper.

twi: Wo tamfo sũa wo asaw a, okyeakyea ne pã.
eng: When one who dislikes you imitates you dancing, he bends his waist sideways.

twi: Otaṅ nni aduru.
eng: There is no medicine to cure hatred.

twi: Wotañ bi a, na wofa ne yere.
eng: When you hate some one, then you seduce his wife.

twi: Wotañ wo nĩ a, womfá no mmã dom.
eng: (Even) if you hate your mother, you do not hand her over to the enemy.

twi: Wo yoŋkõ di wo amĩm na wunni no bi a, na ete se wusuro no.
eng: When your friend helps himself to the larger share (when eating with you) and you (next time you are eating with him) do not do likewise, then it is as if you fear him.

twi: Qyoŋkõ mu wo oyoŋkõ.
eng: Among friends there are some who are (greater) friends (than others).

twi: ‘Yoŋkõ, yoŋkõ,’ na emã asem terew.
eng: ‘Friend, friend (I will tell you a secret),’ that is how news spreads.

twi: Ade to wo ani so a, wo yoŋkõ na oyi mã wo.
eng: When something gets in your eye, it is your friend who removes it for you.

twi: Woko wo yoŋkõ ṅkyeŋ agoru na ne nã pam no a, na ode wo.
eng: When you go to your friend's house to play, and his mother drives him off, it is really you she means (to send home).

twi: Wo ani bere wo yoŋkõ ade a, woye bi, na wunwĩia.
eng: When you covet something belonging to your friend, you work for it, but you do not steal (it).

twi: Okwasea na ose, ‘Wode me yoŋkō, na woŋné me’.
eng: It is the fool who says, ‘They mean my friend, but not me’.

twi: Okwasea na wobu no be a, wokyere no ase.
eng: When the fool is told a proverb, the meaning of it has to be explained to him.

twi: Okwasea, na ne guaŋ tew mpeŋ abieŋ.
eng: It is the fool’s sheep that breaks loose twice.

twi: Okwasea redi ne sika a, ose ne nseŋia ye merew.
eng: When a fool is squandering his gold dust, he says his scales are out of order.

twi: Okwasea ani te a, nã agoru agu.
eng: By the time the fool has learned to play the game, the players have dispersed.

twi: Okwasea unim biribi a, onim ne fufū tow.
eng: If the fool knows nothing else, he (at least) knows all about his plantain dumpling.

twi: Nea wuresisi kwasea no, na onyansafo te ho fīe wo.
eng: Where you are taking advantage of a fool, there a wise man is, looking on at you.

twi: Okwasea na wotew ne ntorowa toŋ no.
eng: It is the fool whose own tomatoes (?) are plucked and sold to him.

twi: Nyansa nye sika na woakyekyere asie.
eng: Wisdom is not gold dust that it should be tied up and put away.

twi: Onyansafo de pesewa gye okwasea nsam' pereguaŋ.
eng: The clever man takes one penny worth of gold dust and receives from the hand of the fool gold dust of the value of £8.

twi: Anyansafo bānu goru a, ntōtō ba.
eng: When two men of equal wisdom play together, discord arises.

twi: Anyansafo bānu kye mensā, obākō daṅ si ho, na obākō redaṅ butuw ho.
eng: When two wise men are dividing up a yam between them, one turns a piece over and puts it down (for the other), but the other again turns it over and exposes the other side.

twi: Obi ṅkyekyere nyansa-kotoku mfa ṅkoto adakam' mmegyina adiho, nse no se, ‘Kyere me asem’.
eng: No one ties up a wisdom-bag, and takes it and puts it away in a box and comes and stands in the courtyard and says, ‘Explain the matter to me’.

twi: Nokware mu nni abra.
eng: In truth there is no deceit.

twi: Nokware nye ahẽ (nnōsō) na woatwa mu ṅkontompo.
eng: There is not so much of truth that it should be cut off by falsehood.

twi: Wutwa ṅkontompo a, wusuro Kumase.
eng: When you tell a lie, you fear Coomassie.

twi: Otɔrofo de mfe apem tu kwan a, onokwafo de dakoro tiw no to no.
eng: Whereas the liar takes a thousand years to go a journey, the one who speaks the truth follows and overtakes him in a day.

twi: Otɔrofo gye agua; ose, ‘Manyã obo’.
eng: Smooth-tongued one take a seat; he says, ‘I have got a stone’.

twi: Otɔrofo na ose, ‘Me dansefo wo Aburokyiri’.
eng: The smooth-tongued one says, ‘My witness is in Europe’.

twi: Wode nkontompo ka asem a, wobere.
eng: When you speak falsehoods in stating a case, you become weary.

twi: Wode nkontompo pe ade mfe apem a, onokwafo de nokware gye wo nsam' dakoro.
eng: When you seek for a thing for one thousand years by the aid of falsehood, the truthful man, using truth, takes it from your grasp in a day.

twi: Atokoro see nokwapem.
eng: One falsehood spoils a thousand truths.

twi: Eha bateni ha pani.
eng: When the hirer is in want, the hireling is in want.

twi: Ehĩa onipa a, ọda wuram'.
eng: When a man is in want, he sleeps in the forest. That is, he is compelled to go far afield, hunting or fishing, in order to find food.

twi: Ehĩa wo a, na worewe sumãnã-dwé.
eng: When in want, then you eat the palm nuts off the refuse heap.

twi: Ehĩa wo a, ṅwu.
eng: When you are in want, do not die. That is, do not give up hope.

twi: ‘Ahĩa me na fịwe mã me,’ nti na obi yee akoa.
eng: ‘I am in want, so look after me,’ it is thus some became slaves, (lit. one became a slave).

twi: Ohĩa, wodi no fie, na wonni no gua so.
eng: When you are a poor man, you remain at home and do not mix in public affairs.

twi: Ohĩa hĩa wo a, woŵe aberekyi wére.
eng: When you are in want, you chew a goat's skin. In times of scarcity the skins of goats and sheep are cut up and boiled.

twi: Ohĩa hĩa wo na wutĩ abeté a, edań' fán.
eng: When you are in want and pick out the maize from the pot, that even turns into a leaf. Roasted maize, which only the poor eat.

twi: Ohia hĩa wo na wotɔ nsu-oŋwinim' a, ɛhye wo.
eng: When you are suffering from poverty and happen to fall into cold water, it scalds you.

twi: Ohia nhyɛ da.
eng: Poverty does not fix on a day (to come upon one), (i. e. its arrival will be unexpected).

twi: Ohia na ɛmã odehye yɛ akoa.
eng: It is poverty that causes the free man to become a slave.

twi: Ohia na ɛmã otwɛa ko anopa-be soo.
eng: It is poverty that causes the dog (i.e. the dog's master) to have to turn out for the early morning palm-nut cutting.

twi: Ohia ne gyimi.
eng: Poverty is stupidity. That is, a poor man is reckoned a fool.

twi: Ohia nni Aburokyiri a, ankã Oburoni ammehata ne ntama Abibirim'.
eng: If there had been no poverty in Europe, then the white man would not have come and spread his cloths in Africa.

twi: Ohĩa te se 'wo, ɛnno fākō.
eng: Poverty is like honey, it is not peculiar to one place alone.

twi: Ohĩa nti na aseredowa sisi abŭrobia so.
eng: It is want that causes the little 'aseredowa' bird to alight on the 'bŭrobia' plant.

twi: Ohĩa tumi nyɛ tumi-pa.
eng: The display of power exhibited by poverty is not real power. A poor man having nothing to lose and becoming desperate, sometimes commits acts which some one having anything at stake would hesitate to do.

twi: Ohĩa yɛ adámmo.
eng: Poverty is madness.

twi: Ohĩa-da na wohũ nipa.
eng: On the day of poverty it is then you perceive who is a man. (a friend)

twi: Ohĩani abāwa koro ṅkyɛ bɛrɛ, nso waṅko a, yennidí.
eng: The poor man's only slave girl soon gets wear, but if she does not go (and work) we do not eat.

twi: Ohĩani bo mfuw.
eng: The poor man does not get in a rage.

twi: Ohĩani bu bɛ a, ɛnhye.
eng: When a poor man makes a proverb, it does not spread abroad.

twi: Ohĩani di powade a, eye se odi dwane.
eng: When a poor man eats something of the value of a halfpenny, it is as if he partakes of a sheep.

twi: Ohĩani fura kyɛmɛ a, eye sẹ efura dunsĩn.
eng: When a poor man wears a silken robe, it is as if it decked a tree stump.

twi: Ohĩani hyẹ sika a, wobu no aẅowa.
eng: When a poor man is decked out in gold, people say it is brass.

twi: Ohĩani nè ọdefo ṅṅoru.
eng: The poor man and the rich man do not play together.

twi: Ohĩani nni biribi a, ọwọ tẹkrẹma a ọde tutu ka.
eng: If the poor man has nothing else, he at least has a tongue with which to defer the payment of his debts.

twi: Ohĩani nni yoṅkõ.
eng: The poor man has no friend.

twi: Ohĩani nom tawa-pa a, eye sẹ tāsẹnfĩ.
eng: When a poor man smokes good tobacco, it is as if he were smoking the remains of some old tobacco in a pipe.

twi: Ohĩani pam akorogow a, na eye no sẹ odidi sãnyãm'.
eng: When the poor man mends his broken wooden bowl, it serves him just as well as if he ate off a pewter dish.

twi: Ohĩani mpaw dabere.
eng: A poor man does not chose his sleeping-place.

twi: Ohĩani aṣem', 'yedi no ntiantiam'.
eng: The complaint a poor man brings is investigated briefly.

twi: Ohĩani asommẹ́n ne batafọsẹ̀.
eng: The poor man's elephant tusk is the wart-hog's tooth.

twi: Ohĩani yane gorọw a, 'yese oyane ńńwahama.
eng: When the poor man wears a necklace of the soft silky 'gorow' leaves, it is said he is wearing a sheep's halter.

twi: Obi mfa ohĩa ntow adọtebẹ.
eng: Not even poverty will make a man fell a palm-tree that stands in a swamp.

twi: Obi mfa ohĩa nsi apempem.
eng: No one can extort from another by using his poverty as a threat.

twi: Obi bọ wo dua se, 'Mã ońwu!' a, ẹnyé yaw sẹ ose, 'Mã ohĩa ńkã no!'
eng: If any one invokes a fetish against you, saying, 'Let this man die', he is not harming you as much as he would were he to say 'Let poverty lay hold on him'.

twi: Wunni ntrama a, na wuse, nsã nyẹ dẹ.
eng: When you have not a cowry shell, then you say that wine is not sweet.

twi: Osikani ne panyin.
eng: The rich man is the elder (i.e. man of importance whose words carry weight in council).

twi: Wonni sika a, ankã wofre no nhwẽa kwa.
eng: If one could not make use of gold dust, then it would merely be called sand.

twi: Sika nni adagyew a, womfa mpe bosea.
eng: When one has just sufficient money for one's own needs, one does not let it out at interest.

twi: Sika nni, ‘Kã wo nsa pe’.
eng: With gold dust (money) it is not (a case of), ‘Put forth your hand and find’.

twi: Sika nko adidi nsan mma kwa.
eng: Money does not go out to earn its livelihood and come back empty-handed (i.e. it earns interest).

twi: Sika kyeŋ nkrante nnam.
eng: Money is sharper than a sword.

twi: Sika pereguan da kŭrom' a, ewo amansan.
eng: If there is a pereguan worth of gold dust in a town, it is for the whole people.

twi: Wo sika resã a, na wo ani tew.
eng: When your gold dust is becoming finished, then you become prudent.

twi: Sika seŋe, biribi anseŋ bio.
eng: Wealth (is) beyond everything, nothing is beyond that again.

twi: Sika te se akoa, woaŋhũ no so fĩe a, oguaŋ.
eng: Gold dust (money) is like unto a slave, if you do not look after it well, it runs away.

twi: Sika ye fe na opegyafo ye nã.
eng: Wealth is a fine thing, but to find an heir is not easy.

twi: Wo sika ye wo yaw a, okom de wo.
eng: If (spending) your money gives you pain, you will go hungry.

twi: Wo sika ye wo yaw na wokõ a, wunyi dom.
eng: If (spending) your money gives you pain and you go to war, you will not win.

twi: Sika-dŭwuma biara nye aniwu.
eng: It is no shame at all to work for money.

twi: Osikafo nom nsã bow a, wofre no yare.
eng: When a sick man is drunk, he is merely said to be unwell.

twi: Osikafo wo ho yi, ofura ntamagow.
eng: When a man is wealthy, he may wear an old cloth.

twi: Osikani de, wonhwãnsĩ no bone ara da.
eng: As for a rich man, he is never sneezed at unluckily.

twi: Sika beŋ wo a, ehoa.
eng: When gold is close to you, it is pale (no longer glitters).

twi: Wunyã ade a, wotaŋ wo ; wunnyã ade a, wofre wo bone.
eng: When you are rich, you are hated ; when you are poor, you are called a bad man.

twi: Ogya a ɛbɛdɛw nɛ ne wisie ṅkɔ.
eng: The fire which is going to blaze up has a different smoke (from other fires).

twi: Ogya a ɛyɛ nnam ṅkyɛ afuw so.
eng: The firewood which is good for fuel does not remain long in the plantation. (It is soon carried home for fuel.)

twi: Ogya dedaw ano nyɛ sɔ-nã.
eng: Wood already touched by fire (and rendered dry) is not hard to set alight.

twi: Ogya hye wo a, woperɛw to wo ba so ansã-na woayi afi no so.
eng: When a spark from the fire burns you, you shake it off on to your child before you (finally) take it off him (again).

twi: Ogya hye wo a, ɛnyɛ wo de, na woretafo.
eng: When fire burns you, you do not find it sweet, but you keep licking the place nevertheless.

twi: Ogya pirɛw a, ɛhye nea ɔda ano.
eng: When a firebrand rolls out from the fire, it burns the one sleeping nearest to it.

twi: Ogya nè atuduru nna.
eng: Fire and gunpowder do not sleep together.

twi: Yenim sɛ wɔde gya bɛko akogu sumăna so, nanso wɔde fi wuram' ba a, wɔde ba ofie ansã.
eng: We know that ash is taken and thrown out on the ash heap, yet when it was brought from the bush (as firewood), it was first of all taken to the house.

twi: Asu a yenni mu adwene no, yemfá mu pow.
eng: From the river whose fish we do not eat, we do not (even) take a nugget.

twi: Asu a wońńuare no, wońnom.
eng: A river (lit. water) you would not bathe in is not drunk from.

twi: Asu et ɛtā hɔ diǹn na ɛfa onipa.
eng: It is the water which stands there calm and silent that drowns (lit. takes) a man.

twi: Asu a ɛte sɛ bosɔ̃rɔpo na ṅkyene atĭwam' yi, na ɛwɔ ase.
eng: A body of water like the great sea, which is so very salt, there must be a reason for that.

twi: Asu biara bɔ po mu a, na ne diṅ ayera.
eng: Whatever the river that falls into the sea, its name is lost.

twi: Asu bɔ biribi diṅ na ɛwɔw.
eng: Water adjures the name of some thing (utters a spell) and then dries up. (Water does not dry up without a cause.)

twi: Asu fa wo a, ɛhɔ ṅhama ṅhĩnā taṅ wo.
eng: When a river is taking you (i. e. drowning you), then all the creepers on its bank (you clutch at) hate you (and will not let you get a hold).

twi: Asu nyiri ṅwam.
eng: A river does not flood out the toucans (which roost on the tops of high trees).

twi: Nsu a wɔde redum gya, wompɛ no kroṅkroṅ.
eng: Clear water is not sought for to quench a fire.

twi: Nsu fa wo a, wonom bi.
eng: When water is drowning you, you nevertheless drink some of it.

twi: Nsu-hunu ye ɔmɛ a, aṅkã akā mfa darewa.
eng: If plain water was satisfying enough, then the fish would not take the hook.

twi: Nsu kye toam' a, eboŋ.
eng: When water remains long in a calabash, it stinks.

twi: Nsu potopoto! tiatia mu na kosaw nsu-pá!
eng: Muddy water! pass through it and go and draw the pure.

twi: Nsu asã asum' nti na osánsá refa apatã.
eng: Because the water has dried up in the river the fish eagle is catching the fish.

twi: Nsu ansõ aguare a, esõ nom.
eng: Water which is not sufficient for bathing in, is sufficient for drinking.

twi: Nsu-nsu ǹhĩnã dõsõ, na bósonopo ne panyin.
eng: Of all the many waters the sea is the old man among them.

twi: Nsu yiri a, na apatã aye ahantaŋ.
eng: When the water is in flood, the fish is proud.

twi: Osu a eto Krobow no, ebi ato Siade.
eng: Of the rain that falls on the Crobo hills some has fallen on the Shai mountains.

twi: Osu boro bo a, etim' nea etim'.
eng: Though rain beats on a stone it (the stone) stands firm where it stands.

twi: Osu ẅe fwo a, wuse, ‘Wafẅe me’, na wunse se, ‘Opetẽẽ me so’.
eng: When the rain beats you, you say, ‘It has beaten me’, but you do not say, ‘It drizzled on me’.

twi: Oso to a, wokum komfo; osu anto a, wokum komfo.
eng: When the rain falls, the fetish priest is killed; (and) when the rain does not fall, the fetish priest is killed.

twi: Oso beto a, mframa na edi kan.
eng: When the rain is going to fall, it is the wind that comes first.

twi: Oso ato aboro asense, ‘Monnserew me, me hṍ bewo’.
eng: The rain has fallen (and) beat on the ‘asense’ fowl (and she says), ‘You need not laugh at me, I shall get dry’.

twi: Osu to fẅe wo na oẅia fi hye wo a, na wuhṹ abrabṍ yaw.
eng: When the rain falls and beats upon you and the sun comes forth and scorches you, then you behold (as it were) the troubles of life.

twi: Osu to gu po mu.
eng: The rain falls, pouring into the sea.

twi: Oso to na egu biribi so ansã-na ekã wo a, enyé yaw.
eng: When the rain falls and drops on something else first before touching you, it does not hurt.

twi: Osu to anadwo na woanhũ a, adekyẽẽ, woanhũ fam ana?
eng: When the rain falls at night and you have not known of it, at dawn have you not seen the ground?

twi: Obi abusudé yẹ obi akăradé.
eng: What is bad luck for one man is good luck for another.

twi: Obi busuyefoo ne bi nipa-pa.
eng: A knave for one is a good man for another.

twi: Obi ade-dedaw ko obi nsam' a, eye no foforo.
eng: When an old thing belonging to one person gets into the hands of another, it becomes a new thing for him.

twi: Obi afom akum a, wo nso mfom ṅṅua!
eng: When some one has killed something by mistake, as for you, do not flay it by mistake!

twi: Obi fre wo Sẹwósé a, mpe ntem nserew; ebia wo agya ye obonnātőfő.
eng: If some one remarks you are like your father, do not be in too great a hurry to laugh (i.e. be flattered); for all you know, your father may have been a ravisher of women.

twi: Obi afuw ső a, womfá mpampā na efow.
eng: Though some one may have a very large plantation, that is not to say people are to bring their bowls and loot.

twi: Obi gyina obi'mati, na ohũ-guam'.
eng: When one stands on another's shoulders, then he sees over the market.

twi: Obi kwaṅ ṅkyẹ na esi bi de mu.
eng: One man's road does not go far without meeting another's.

twi: Obi kye wo ade a, (na) woda n'ase.
eng: When some one gives you a present, (then) you thank him.

twi: Obi mfa obi ade ṅhoahoa nehõ.
eng: No one boasts of what belongs to another.

twi: Obi mfa ọbomũ ṅhow gya so.
eng: No one takes a whole animal and dries it over a fire.

twi: Obi mfa ade ṅkoyi mmusu wo kŭrotia, na ọsaṅ ṅkofa bio.
eng: No one places his propitiatory offering at the entrance of the village, and turns back again to remove it.

twi: Obi mfa adidi mfa adepe.
eng: One cannot both feast and become rich.

twi: Obi mfa dọkonsín kwáŋkyeŋ mmisa nea otwaa so.
eng: One does not take half a loaf from the wayside and then inquire who cut the other half.

twi: Obi mfa fere ńware obi ne nua a ne pãm pow.
eng: No one, lest he should be called shy, would marry some one's sister who had a lump at the base of her spine.

twi: Obi mfa ahina hunu mu ńkyere opanyin.
eng: One does not show the inside of an empty pot to an elder.

twi: Obi mfa ńhõma nto nsu mu ńko ahemfi.
eng: One does not put a hide in water and then go off to the king's palace (where one has been summoned).

twi: Obi mfa hyirew ntiw nea watɔ wuram'.
eng: No one takes white clay and follows some one who has run off to the forest (in order to rub it on him).

twi: Obi mfa amanne a wahũ ntutu kaw.
eng: No one tells how bad a state his affairs are really in, when asking for time to settle a debt.

twi: Obi mfa n'afuru mmutuw bŭropatá so na ne mfefo ntwẽtwẽ mfa n'ase.
eng: No one uses his own belly to cover up his corn store, that his friends may pull some out from under him.

twi: Obi mfa ne naṅ abieṅ nsusu asu.
eng: No one tests the depth of a river with both his feet.

twi: Obi mfa ne nsa beṅkum ṅkyere n'agya amamfɔ so.
eng: No one takes his left hand to point out his father's old village.

twi: Obi mfa ne nsa nto bi anom' na ɔmpae n'atifĩ.
eng: No one puts his finger in another man's mouth and then beats him over the head.

twi: Obi mfa ne sẽ mmobɔ adwẽ mmã ne yɔŋkɔ.
eng: No one cracks a palm nut with his own teeth and gives it to his companion.

twi: Obi mfa toamũm mfa ṅkosẽre ṅno.
eng: No one takes a calabash without an opening in it to go and ask for palm oil.

twi: Obi mfi agyama so mma fam' mmepe okótokoro.
eng: No one descends from the 'gyama' shrub to the ground and then says he wants a forked stick.

twi: Obi ṅwɛfɛwɛɛ odabere na ade ṅkyɛe da.
eng: No one ever kept looking for a sleeping-place (and continued the search) till dawn.

twi: Obi ṅhintaw nsɔ gya.
eng: No one hides himself and (then) lights a fire.

twi: Obi ṅhinti prɛkɔ mmɔ ahina.
eng: No one breaks the water-pot the first time he stumbles.

twi: Obi ṅhũ ‘Aṅkănă’, ṅkita ‘N’aṅkănă’, nnyā ‘N’aṅkănă’, na onse se, ‘Mihũi a, aṅkănă’.
eng: No one who has seen ‘Had I known, I should not . . .’, who has laid hold of ‘Had I known, I should not . . .’, who has (ever) possessed ‘Had I known, I should not . . .’, would ever say (again) ‘Had I known, I should not . . .’

twi: Obi ṅhũ nimdeɛ ṅko ayi (ase) na okosore a, waserew.
eng: No one has any sense (who) goes to attend a funeral custom, and on rising up to take his departure, laughs.

twi: Obi ṅhũ onipa dakoro nse no se, ‘Woafon’.
eng: One does not see a man for one day only (or for the first time), and say to him, ‘You have become thin’.

twi: Obi ṅhũ onipa aẅia na anadẅo onso kanea ṅfẅe n’anim.
eng: No one sees a man by day and at night lights a lamp to look at his face.

twi: Obi ṅko obi akurā ṅkyere n’ase.
eng: One man does not go to the village of another and tell (the chief of that village) its origin (history).

twi: Obi ṅkɔ́ obi kũrom' ṅkofrɛ nehɔ̃ se, ‘Agyeman’.
eng: One does not go to another's village and call himself ‘Agyeman’.

twi: Obi ṅkɔ́ ahũã ná oṅkã ṅkwã̃.
eng: No one (who) goes begging a meal is the one to serve out the soup.

twi: Obi aṅko ná obi amma a, aṅkã yebeye deŋ ahũ se okwaṅ mu nye?
eng: If no one had gone and no one had come, what should we have done to find out if the road were safe (or not)?

twi: Obi ṅkose se, ‘Putu ṅhyew! Putu hyew a, yehũã bi adi’.
eng: No one says (when the yam store is on fire), ‘Let the yam store burn! When it does we shall scrape roasted yams to eat’.

twi: Obi ṅkotew bisekyim mfa mfra bisetoro ṅkotoṅ mmã ne mãnn.
eng: No one picks good kola nuts and mixes them with spurious ones and goes and sells them to his own countrymen.

twi: Obi nkwati kokũrobeti mmo pow.
eng: No one dispenses with the thumb in tying a knot.

twi: Obi ṅkyerɛ obi se, ‘To ṅkyene di’.
eng: No one shows another, saying, ‘Buy salt and eat’.

twi: Obi nnim a, obi kyerɛ.
eng: If one man does not know, another man explains.

twi: Obi nnim adekyɛe mu asem.
eng: No one knows the story of to-morrow's dawn.

twi: Obi mpɛ obi yiye.
eng: No one wishes well for another.

twi: Obi ntó ntasu nto fam’, mfa ne tɛkrɛma mfa.
eng: No one expectorates on the ground and then takes his tongue and licks it up (lit. takes it up).

twi: Obi ntwɛn Firaw ansã-na wahoro ne tãm.
eng: No one waits (to reach) the Volta river before washing his cloth.

twi: Obi se, obɛsoa wo a, wunse se, ‘Mɛnantew’.
eng: When some one says he will carry you, you do not say, ‘I shall walk’.

twi: Obi se ɔkyeɛ wo amirika a, huruw fĩe kwaṅkyeɛ, na fa akyiri nè anim to no ho.
eng: When some one says he can run faster than you, jump (and) fall to

twi: Obi seŋ wo a, mã oŋseŋ wo; na oŋo nso wo obi a oseŋ no.
eng: When some one excels you, let him excel you; as for him, he again has some one who excels him.

twi: Biribiara nye yaw se aniwu.
eng: There is nothing that hurts like shame.

twi: Biribi wo soro a, etiv̌a se ebeba fam'.
eng: Whatever is above must come down to the earth.

twi: ‘Bo me na memmo wo,’ nye agoru.
eng: ‘Hit me, but I must not hit you,’ is not play.

twi: Wobo ahina ho a, na wuhu nea okãm da.
eng: When you tap the pot, you see where the crack is.

twi: Wode tekrema si awowa a, wuntumi mpoŋ no.
eng: When you place your tongue in pawn, you cannot redeem it. (A word once spoken cannot be unsaid.)

twi: Ade ketewa na wode susuw kese.
eng: It is a small thing that is taken to measure a big thing.

twi: Ade-pa na etoŋ neho.
eng: The good thing sells itself.

twi: Ade yera a, na ɛwɔ nipa nsam'.
eng: When a thing is lost, then it is in some one else's hand (possession).

twi: Wo ade yɛ fɛ a, obi na ɔkã kyerɛ wo, na ɛnyɛ woankasa na wokã.
eng: When you possess something that is beautiful, it is some one else who tells you (so) and not you yourself who speak (about it).

twi: Wo de anyɛ yiye a, woŋkofa obi de nye wo de.
eng: When what you have is not good, you do not go and take what belongs to some one else.

twi: Dua a ɛbɛwɔ wo ani no, wobu so, na wonseɛ ano.
eng: You break off the point of the stick that is about to pierce your eye; you do not sharpen the point.

twi: Dua a ɛtɔ nãm na ano hyew.
eng: It is the stick that the meat is roasted on that gets the end burned.

twi: Dua biara nsow nnyã ǹfĩwiren da.
eng: No tree ever bore fruit without first having flowers.

twi: Dua biakɔ nye kwae.
eng: One tree does not make a forest.

twi: Dua mfa mfe aduasã ǹkyea, na womfa afe koro ntɛe no.
eng: A tree does not grow bent for thirty years that one should (expect to) straighten it in one.

twi: Dua kẹse bu a, brofere na esi anaŋmu.
eng: When a great tree breaks (and falls), the papaw tree takes its place.

twi: Dua kẹse bu a, ne mma bubu wo ne hō kwa.
eng: When a great tree has fallen, its children (young shoots or seeds) burst forth from it in vain. (They will soon die once the sap has dried up.)

twi: Dua si akurā a, ne ntini wo fie.
eng: When a tree stands in a small village, its roots are in the houses.

twi: Dua taŋ wo a, na ebu bo wo.
eng: When a tree hates you, it breaks (and) falls on you.

twi: Womfá ade anum nto aduonum hō.
eng: Four things are not compared with forty.

twi: Wo fi ne wo fi.
eng: Your house is your own house.

twi: Afisẹm nye atamagow na woasi ahatá gua sò.
eng: A private matter is not like the old cloth that has been spread to dry in the market-place.

twi: Wobeforo dua a, wofi n'ase na womfi soro.
eng: When one would climb a tree, one begins from the bottom and not from the top.

twi: Mframa mmae a, na fĩwereɛ mu ye krãnã.
eng: It is before the wind comes that the long grass is motionless.

twi: Afuw mu nni biribi a, ɛwɔ krãnãnã.
eng: If a plantation has nothing else in it, it has at least silence.

twi: Agoru, wogoro no tipɛn.
eng: Play, you play with one your own size.

twi: Ahina hɔ hyɛhyɛ no, na nsu na ɛwom'.
eng: When the surface of a pot glistens, that is because there is water on it.

twi: Ahina bɔ a, na kora ata hɔ.
eng: When the water-pot breaks, the calabash in it remains (unharmed) beside it.

twi: Wo hɔ ye dɛn a, wonyɛ bānu adwuma.
eng: Though you may be strong, you do not do two men's work.

twi: Wo hɔ nye dɛn a, na wuse, ‘Kahiri nye’.
eng: When you are not strong, then you say, ‘The head-rest is no good’.

twi: Ahõofe ntua kaw.
eng: Personal beauty does not pay a debt.

twi: Wohye afiri a, wuŋwu agyaŋ.
eng: When you stand on (fall in?) a trap (and are killed), you do not die from an arrow (wound).

twi: Wokaŋ nantwi a, wokaŋ ne dùa.
eng: When you count cattle, you count their tails.

twi: Woko obi fi, na okotow ho a, wummisa no agua.
eng: When you go to some one else's house, and the owner is squatting there on the ground, you do not ask him for a stool.

twi: Woko kũrow bi mu na wuse, ‘Mammeto nnipa bi wo ha’ a, wose wo se, ‘Yeaŋhũ oniŋa a waba’.
eng: If you go to some one else's town and say, ‘I have not met any one here so far (of importance)’, they (the town's people will retort and) say, ‘We have not been aware that some one has come (to our town)’.

twi: Woŋkoo obi afum' da a, wuse, ‘Me ŋko ne kùafó.
eng: If you never went to any one else's farm, (you would) say, ‘I alone am a farmer’.

twi: Yekum bi ansã-na yeapam bi.
eng: Some are killed before others are put to flight.

twi: Woŋkúm mmarima a, womfá mmea.
eng: If the men are not slain, the women are not carried off.

twi: Okwaŋ a wunsuro mu, na aboa kyere wo mu.
eng: It is the path you do not fear that the wild beast catches you on.

twi: Okwantenni nim asɛm-kã, na onnim asekyerɛ.
eng: The traveller (may) tell all he has seen (on his journey), but he cannot explain (all).

twi: Okwaŋ wɔ asõ.
eng: A path has ears.

twi: Ǹkyene fi nsum' na woḥata, na wode gu nsum' ho ara bio.
eng: Salt is procured (by evaporation) from water, yet it is taken and put back there in the water again.

twi: Ǹkyene nse nehõ se, ‘Meye de’.
eng: Salt does not address itself and say, ‘I am agreeable (to the taste)’.

twi: Akyene anim da ho a, wonnyae nyaŋ ṅkyeŋ.
eng: When the face of a drum is there (to beat), you do not leave that to beat the side.

twi: Wokyere onipa akunse na wokum no a, enye no yaw.
eng: When you have a just reason for seizing a man and killing him, you do not hurt him (by doing so).

twi: Nãm nni ho nti na wode mmere ye ṅkwaŋ.
eng: It is because there is no meat that mushrooms are taken to make soup.

twi: Nea wadi bem nsoaa oguaŋ du.
eng: He who has won his case never yet carried the sheep.

twi: Wunnim asaw a, na wuse, ‘Akyene nye de’.
eng: When you do not know how to dance, then you say, ‘The drum is not sounding sweetly’.

twi: Wo nua sĕrẹ sŏ a, na ẹnyẹ wo na woda so.
eng: Your sister's thigh may be plump, but it is not you who lie on it.

twi: Nsátéā biakŏ butuw fa ade wọ fam’ a, entumi.
eng: If one finger tries to pick up something from the ground, it cannot.

twi: Asẹm a wọkã serew wọ bãbi na wọkã sũ wọ bãbi.
eng: A matter which in one place is a subject of mirth, in another place is the cause of tears.

twi: Asẹm a wobese na wobẹsaŋ no, fa sã mã ẹŋka wo tirim.
eng: A word that when spoken you would wish back, let it remain (unspoken) in your head.

twi: Asẹm-pa nye ọkã-nã.
eng: A good case is not difficult to state.

twi: Asẹŋ-kese bẹba a, ofraŋkã nsi so.
eng: When some really big business is on hand, no flag is flown.

twi: Woso adaka a, na woso ne mu ade.
eng: When a box is carried, what is inside the box is carried.

twi: Asɔ̃ te sɛ nsɛña; woto mu to mu a, ɛda.
eng: The ears are like a pair of scales; when more and more are put in, they are weighted down (lit. sleep).

twi: Osram de bɛrɛbɛrɛ na etwa ɔman mu.
eng: The moon moves slowly, but it crosses the town.

twi: Ata-panyin nni ṅkyene mmã ɛntere ata-k̃īmā anom'.
eng: The elder twin does not eat salt that it may trickle into the younger's mouth.

twi: Wo ntama biri a, wohoro, na wonhyew.
eng: When your cloth is dirty you wash it, but you do not burn it.

twi: Wote nsu hɔ reguare na obɔdamfo fa wo tãm a, fwefwe bi ansã-na woatiw no; nà wumfura bi a, obi besusuw se mo bãnu ye abɔdamfo.
eng: When you are down bathing at the water and a madman runs off with your cloth, look for another before you follow him, for if you follow him naked, some one will suppose you are both of you mad.

twi: Tete abɛ, womfá nye ṅkwaṅ.
eng: Old palm nuts are not used to make soup.

twi: Tete ara ne nne.
eng: History repeats itself. Lit. The very same ancient (things) are to-day.

twi: Eti nye brofere na woapae mu ahũ mu asɛm.
eng: The head is not the papaw fruit that it should be broken to see the thoughts inside.

twi: Owia wo soro na ehyehye sã yi, na menné se ebebeṅ fam.
eng: The sun is up above and it can burn like this, but how much more (could it scorch) if it came down near to earth.

twi: Wiase wotrã no bãnu bãnu.
eng: In the world all things are two and two.

twi: Obi ṅkyi koko na onni ne mma.
eng: No one makes a fowl taboo and then eats its chickens.

twi: Obi ṅkyi pete nni ne ṅkesua.
eng: No one makes a vulture taboo and then eats its eggs.

twi: Aduaṅ bi a wuṅhũũ bi da wo wo nã nè wo agya muka so no, na nea wukyi neṅ.
eng: Some food, the like of which you have never seen on your mother's or your father's cooking hearth, that is the kind you make taboo.

twi: Nea ahõodeṅ kyi ne kọm.
eng: What strength makes taboo is hunger.

twi: Obi nsõ dae, ṅkọ nea wọbekum no.
eng: No one dreams of going to where they will kill him.

twi: Tete ka asõm'.
eng: Ancient things remain in the ears. (Tradition survives).
